Jet lag isn’t just for travelers hurtling across time zones. Migratory birds may get it, too.
Manx shearwaters (Puffinus puffinus) fly fast enough to experience jet lag, researchers report October 29 in Science. Decades of tracking data from foraging flights revealed that rapid east-west journeys can throw the seabirds’ internal clocks out of sync with local time, causing them to misjudge the sun’s position and veer slightly off course.
For animals crossing vast oceans, the sun can help them determine which direction to fly. But because the sun’s position in the sky changes throughout the day, these animals need an internal clock synchronized with natural local sun time to use it as a compass. This circadian rhythm helps them compensate for the sun’s apparent movement and stay on course.
But when birds zip east or west, local time shifts faster than their internal clocks might adjust. Scientists have long predicted that this mismatch could confound the birds’ sun-based compasses, but testing the idea in the wild “has seemed impossible until now,” says Tim Guilford, a biologist at the University of Oxford.
Over 20 years, Guilford and colleagues equipped 1,045 breeding Manx shearwaters with miniature GPS trackers. The trackers logged thousands of trips from United Kingdom breeding colonies to feeding grounds up to 1,000 kilometers away. The team focused on the return journeys, isolating 1,837 continuous homeward flights.
Assuming the seabirds’ internal clocks were synchronized with local time at sunrise, the researchers calculated how flights should throw off their sun compass and compared those predictions with GPS tracking data. The birds veered as expected, by as much as 15 degrees from their intended direction.
“But what really surprised us is that the small orientation errors … continue to be visible even when the birds were in sight of presumably familiar land,” Guilford says. While following a coastline, the birds should be able to use it as a guide to keep their course. But they either veered closer to shore or farther out to sea in line with their predicted sun compass errors. The pattern suggests that the birds use the sun compass alongside coastal cues, even when the two point in different directions.
The errors are small enough that they add only a few kilometers to the journey, not enough to prevent the Manx shearwaters from finding their way home.
This navigational tug-of-war excites Sangeeta Rani, a chronobiologist at the University of Lucknow in India. The findings, Rani says, hint at an ability that could serve these feathered fliers well as climate change and human activities alter familiar landscapes: The birds seem to process and integrate multiple navigational cues without relying blindly on any one of them.
“After all, if I have marked a path for myself in the woods, my innate ability is not to mindlessly follow the markings,” Rani says. “It is to find out what’s missing and still find my way back.”

64ce921a4adf.text: After his far-right coalition lost 11 seats in the election, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is trying to discredit the results by claiming there was mass voting fraud in Arab communities. Why it matters: Netanyahu appears to be trying to spook the opposition bloc out of cooperating with Arab parties to form a new government. But the opposition is concerned he has an even more ambitious goal: To prevent the results from being certified at all. That would block the swearing in of a new parliament, in which he would lose his majority. Driving the news: Netanyahu and his Likud party started the campaign to delegitimize the Arab vote days before the elections. Half of Netanyahu's social media posts on Election Day cast suspicion on the unprecedented turnout in Arab communities, an apparent attempt to drive his supporters to the polls. Arab voters cast ballots in historic numbers, winning 19 seats between their two parties. On Wednesday, Netanyahu's Likud party issued a statement claiming the "elections were stolen" by the Arab parties through bribes and fraud. Its claims were based on the arrest of three activists from the Arab Ra'am party who were suspected of paying a small number of voters in one of the Arab cities. The Israeli police said there was no evidence to support Likud's claims of a "stolen" election. Behind the scenes: The situation escalated dramatically on Thursday when a letter sent to the director of the Shin Bet domestic security agency was leaked to Israel's Channel 12. It was written by the supreme court judge who heads the Central Elections Committee. The judge ordered the Shin Bet director to immediately investigate suspicions of election interference by foreign countries and submit conclusions within a week. Shortly after the letter leaked, Israeli media outlets identified Qatar as the country in question. The allegation is that it funneled money to one of the Arab parties to propel turnout in their communities. Over the past year, several of Netanyahu's closest advisers have been investigated by Shin Bet for allegedly being paid by Qatar to improve its image among Israelis. Zoom in: At a press conference on Election Day, the Shin Bet director, who is a far-right Netanyahu political appointee, said the elections were "safe and secure." He did not mention any suspected foreign interference. But the next day, the director met the head of the Central Elections Committee and briefed him on intelligence that suggested foreign countries sent money to one of the Arab parties to increase turnout. Later that day, the Shin Bet director briefed Netanyahu on the intelligence, but not his opponent Gadi Eisenkot. Eisenkot was briefed by the Shin Bet only after the letter leaked. Later on Thursday, the director also briefed outgoing opposition leader Yair Lapid. Sources with knowledge say the Shin Bet had the intelligence weeks before the elections. In a statement on Thursday, Shin Bet said the head of the Central Elections Committee was the only one outside of the security agency who knew about the investigation ahead of the elections . Zoom out: Shin Bet said in its statement that the investigation is "focused and narrowly defined" and made clear it doesn't cast doubt on the vote of the Arab minority. "The investigation should not be used to cast suspicion on or accuse an entire sector of society that exercised its democratic and legal right to vote. Only those who acted unlawfully will be held accountable," the statement read. What they're saying: But Netanyahu and Likud nevertheless seized on it. After the letter leaked on Thursday, they called it "an earthquake" and again claimed without evidence that "the elections were stolen." "This is an attack on democracy aimed at enabling a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of right-wing rule in order to bring about an Israeli withdrawal and the defeat of the IDF on all fronts — first and foremost in Iran," the Likud said. It also said that "no Zionist party should cooperate" with the Arab parties in replacing the Knesset speaker after the new parliament is sworn in or in establishing a new government. The other side: Eisenkot said the suspicions of foreign interference in the elections must be immediately and thoroughly investigated. But the swearing-in of the Knesset must proceed as scheduled, he said. "Netanyahu is leading an illegitimate influence campaign targeting the Israeli public, aimed at delaying the publication of the election results and manufacturing a false narrative to delegitimize the new Knesset," Eisenkot said. What to watch: The vote count ended on Thursday with the opposition parties winning 67 seats and Netanyahu's coalition winning 53. The results are expected to be certified next week, with the Knesset being sworn in several days later. The opposition plans to immediately replace the current speaker of the Knesset and start passing laws — first and foremost, establishing a national commission to investigate the security failures that led to the October 7 attacks. Netanyahu has blocked efforts to launch such an inquiry for three years. Yes, but: While the opposition's majority will allow it to take over parliament, it's not clear whether it will be able to assemble a government. Doing so would require the support of the Arab parties — and not all opposition parties want to join forces with them.

Can inertial navigation make ground-robot swarms real?
Two startups are equipping small wheeled robots with a GPS-free nav package.
Two startups, working together for just under a week, may have found a way around the biggest obstacle to deploying swarms of ground robots: the need for GPS-free navigation in a small package.
Swarmbotics AI, which makes 100-pound autonomous robots, is teaming up with TERN, whose navigation software doesn’t need GPS, the companies announced Wednesday.
The Army has been seeking alternatives to the spoofable, jammable satellite-based system for years.
“The current environment has taught us that GPS is the first thing that gets canned on the battle space,” William Shuart, a program manager for the Army’s Pathfinder3D program, told Army magazine in January.
So the service is fielding jam-resistant GPS cards for munitions and is also working on ALTNAV, which uses a different satellite constellation. But its plans for a robot-forward ground force require a position-navigation-timing system that can get by without a satellite signal at all. The self-driving car industry, with its reliance on GPS and unstealthy LiDAR, hasn’t been much help.
Enter TERN, whose PNT system needs no signals from space, and Swarmbotics AI, an Arizona robotics company whose four-wheeled FireAnts fit roughly into a two-foot cube.
“Our teams integrated the TERN system on site here in Phoenix into the FireAnt in less than a week, which I think is really impressive. So we went from never having really spoken to these guys on a technical level at least to having the system fielded in a week,” said Drew Watson, co-founder and CTO of Swarmbotics AI.
TERN’s Independently Derived Positioning System, or IDPS, combines input from the vehicle’s own sensors, including “wheel speed, steering angle, and 3D motion data,” with onboard map data.
“We’re using the motion of that vehicle all the way down to something as as compact as a FireAnt, and through that successive motion, we're able to output latitude and longitude at the same rate that GPS could, or twice a second,” said Shaun Moore, co-founder and CEO of TERN.
Next up: sharing that information, which Watson described as “a building block to something else.” The team wants to move toward coordinated swarm maneuvering, with teams of robots sharing data with one another in a mesh network. If each member of the swarm understands where it is and where its teammates are, that data can add value to other sensor data, such as camera or radar feeds about threats.
“The way that's working is that each one of these FireAnts is giving a line of bearing to an enemy tank, for instance. Those are triangulated into a position of that enemy tank via multiple firings. The quality of that identification, the position of that enemy tank, is based on the position of the firings…It improves the automatic target recognition,” said Watson.
Both companies have already drawn Army attention. TERN received a $11.26 million contract in September, and both have participated in the service’s Operation Jailbreak tech demonstrations.

da0b9ab94110.text: By — Laurie Kellman, Associated Press Laurie Kellman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/cnn-msnow-and-politico-ask-court-to-make-trump-access-order-permanent Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter CNN, MSNOW and Politico ask court to make Trump access order permanent Politics Oct 29, 2026 1:10 PM EDT Three news outlets have beefed up their legal complaint against the White House over access, saying it is continuing to defy a judge's orders by refusing to let them return to covering President Donald Trump in the Oval Office and on Air Force One — thus violating their free speech rights by continuing to keep them out of the rotating press "pool." CNN, MSNOW and Politico said Wednesday that the president is retaliating against them for reports he does not like, which violates U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly's previous orders for the administration to allow reporters for the outlets to fully return to the pool of journalists covering the president. WATCH: Attorney for banned outlets on legal fight over White House press access Even after those orders, the White House was continuing to block reporters for those outlets from covering Trump in "the very locations that the president most frequently engages with the press," Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., the outlets' attorney, said in a statement. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The most recent filing asks the court to make those previous orders permanent. At issue is whether the president, or anyone, can punish news outlets for the content of their reports. The news organizations say that doing so is "viewpoint discrimination" forbidden by the First Amendment's free-speech protections. READ MORE: Judge extends order blocking Trump from banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from White House Trump insists that he doesn't have to let news outlets whose reports he dislikes onto White House grounds, on Air Force One or other areas. The White House had not responded to the amended lawsuit as of Thursday morning. "Every news organization now faces the risk of similar punishment for coverage the President deems insufficiently favorable," the outlets wrote in their filing, "and the public is deprived of current and complete information about its government." The filing comes about two weeks after Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in the extraordinary case pitting the president against the news outlets that cover him. READ MORE: CNN says it was left off Air Force One for Trump's Saturday trip to a college football game In a victory for the journalists, Kelly expanded a previous, temporary ruling that the administration had violated the news outlets' Fifth Amendment right to due process. On Oct. 13, Kelly also sided with a second argument by the outlets: that Trump's ban breached their First Amendment right to free speech. Kelly rejected Trump's reasoning that the ban was driven by policy goals, such as protecting national security. He argued the ban was the result of Trump's stated belief that the outlets' reporting was inaccurate and biased. "Simply put," Kelly wrote in the opinion, "That is unlawful viewpoint discrimination" — the government taking action against types of speech or coverage it does not like. These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.
With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.
The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).
“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.
To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.
Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.
“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.
As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.
It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.
The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.
“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

Health officials from 45 African countries met Wednesday to coordinate a continent-wide response to an Ebola outbreak that has killed nearly 5,000 people in DR Congo and spread to Kenya and Nigeria, as an assessment presented at the meeting showed only three of 31 countries evaluated were adequately prepared to respond.
âOur member states, they agree and they commit to implement all actions that we discussed today, including strengthening the preparedness efforts,â said Jean Kaseya, head of Africa CDC, the continentâs public health agency. 1f1b043426ef.text: By — Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/inflation-heats-up-again-days-before-midterm-elections Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Inflation heats up again, days before midterm elections Economy Oct 29, 2026 12:24 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — An inflation gauge closely monitored by the Federal Reserve accelerated last month, showing that prices remain elevated less than a week before midterm elections in which the uncomfortably high cost of living for millions of Americans has become a central issue. Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May. READ MORE: U.S. economy grows at brisk 3.4% pace in third quarter on strong consumer spending and AI investment Rising gas prices drove much of the inflation increase as renewed violence in the Middle East has kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, up from below $70 before the Iran war. But prices also rose outside of fuel costs. The cost of services such as shipping, hotel rooms, and utilities increased rapidly from August to September, a sign that inflation is spreading and growing more entrenched. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The inflation outlook has become more concerning," Ksenia Bushmeneva, an economist at TD, a bank, wrote in a commentary on the report. "Price pressures are showing signs of heating up. Elevated gasoline prices are keeping headline inflation hot, but underlying pressures are also broadening." WATCH: Warsh holds briefing after Fed leaves key interest rate unchanged Polls show that the rise in inflation has soured most voters on the economy, leading them to give President Donald Trump poor marks on handling rising prices. Trump campaigned in 2024 on lowering the cost of living, including bringing the cost of gas below $2 a gallon. It currently averages about $4.25 a gallon nationwide. Excluding the volatile energy and food categories, core inflation also picked up last month. It increased 3.1% from a year ago in September, up from 3% in August, the Commerce Department said. And from August to September, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the previous month. Separately, the government also said the economy grew at a strong 3.4% annual rate in the July-September quarter, much faster than the 2.2% growth in the April-June quarter, as consumer spending jumped and business investment rose, fueled by spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure. READ MORE: Trump promised to stop inflation. Now Republicans may pay the price in the midterm elections Consumer spending climbed 3.8% at an annual rate in the third quarter, the second straight quarter of strong growth and far above the 0.7% increase in the first three months of the year. Yet there are signs that consumers may struggle to maintain that level of spending. Inflation is eroding their incomes: In September, inflation-adjusted incomes, after taxes, declined 0.3% from the previous month. Consumers appear to be dipping into savings or relying on credit to fuel much of their consumption. "Together with higher borrowing costs, these headwinds are likely to weigh on consumer demand in the coming quarters," Bushmeneva said." The reports come a day after the Federal Reserve, the agency tasked with combatting inflation, left its key interest rate unchanged. Yet strong economic growth and persistently higher prices could mean more pain for Americans when the Fed meets in December. The Fed is much more likely to hike its key interest rate, which could lift borrowing costs across the economy. Thursday's inflation data comes from the personal consumption expenditures price index, which typically echoes the better-known consumer price index published earlier this month. The Fed more closely monitors the PCE index because it puts less weight on housing prices and allows for changes in consumers' shopping habits. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 9ea74f06ca6c.text: By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press By — Julia Frankel, Associated Press Julia Frankel, Associated Press By — Koral Saeed, Associated Press Koral Saeed, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/netanyahus-party-claims-israeli-election-stolen-as-results-show-him-losing-majority Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Netanyahu's party claims Israeli election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority World Oct 29, 2026 8:44 PM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party on Thursday amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had "stolen" the election, potentially with foreign assistance, as final results showed his bloc had lost its majority in parliament. The opposition accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population after a historic showing by Arab-led parties in an attempt to delegitimize the election. If the rest of the opposition teams up with Arab parties, a rare and politically risky move, they could potentially form a majority government in parliament, the Knesset. WATCH: Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us Results released by election officials on Thursday showed Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member assembly, well below the 68 seats it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament. His main opposition won 48 seats and Arab-led parties secured the other 19. The count is complete, but the results still need to be certified and submitted to the country's president next Wednesday. Commission to look into possible foreign interference Netanyahu's party, Likud, has been spreading claims of malfeasance by Arab-led parties since exit polls indicated the prime minister had suffered a setback in Tuesday's vote. But it ramped up the rhetoric after the head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that "serious suspicions" of foreign interference had been brought before him. In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims. But given their serious nature, he asked the agency to investigate. Netanyahu's party responded with an inflammatory statement: "The elections in Israel have been stolen!" it said, claiming — without evidence — that the alleged election interference was "aimed at facilitating a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and toppling of the right wing government." Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu's party were accusing Qatar — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group. Qatar issued a quick denial, calling the allegations "ridiculous and dangerous." As it announced its results early Friday, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. In a video statement, the commission's acting director general, Dean Livne, did not elaborate, but warned that reports about the probe had been "entirely unfounded." "It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population," he said. Netanyahu's opponents accuse him of undermining vote Netanyahu's main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, said Likud was trying to delegitimize the results. "They are doing this because they lost," he said. Eisenkot ridiculed the accusation of foreign interference with a tongue-in-cheek statement, saying: "I welcome the fact that Netanyahu is finally condemning Qatari involvement in the State of Israel." Netanyahu has long faced accusations that former top aides of his accepted money from Qatar. By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be positioning himself to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties, who could potentially give Eisenkot the backing he needs to oust Netanyahu. The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to "cast aspersions" on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner." The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament. It said that even though an investigation was taking place, "allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless." The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week. Netanyahu campaigned on anti-Arab sentiment Even ahead of the vote, Netanyahu and Likud painted the Arab-led parties as a danger to Israel, which critics called an attempt to further marginalize Arab citizens. Arab citizens of Palestinian descent make up 20% of the population but are often viewed with suspicion because of their sympathies with other Palestinians. Those campaign attacks, along with anger over the divisive Netanyahu and his far-right government, brought outraged Arabs to the polls like never before. On Thursday, Yair Golan, head of the Democrats party, accused Netanyahu of "attempting to undermine the election results through an ugly delegitimization campaign directed against the will of the public — and against the Arab public in particular." "Netanyahu is working to steal the election," the Arab-led Joint List party asserted Thursday. The head of the Arab-led Ra'am party, Mansour Abbas, welcomed the investigation into election interference and said his party had nothing to do with the case, while accusing Netanyahu of a campaign of incitement. President Isaac Herzog called it a "sensitive moment" and called for a full investigation. He warned that "we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy." 17b6c0241a01.text: Crypto exchange Binance is investigating what could be the biggest crypto hack in history as users saw upwards of $5.7 billion in funds drained from wallets Thursday afternoon. Why it matters : The suspected hack comes after a wave of high-profile cyberattacks and data breaches during so-called "Black October," when a series of hacks and AI-discovered bugs triggered fears of a global crisis. Driving the news: Binance co-founder Changpeng "CZ" Zhao, who is no longer an executive at the company, said on X that the crypto exchange appears to have been hacked, although a company spokesperson says it's still investigating the matter. Analysts and traders who follow the crypto markets closely estimate that $1.7 billion to $5.7 billion was taken during the suspected cyberattack. "This is unprecedented," said Kevin March, a co-founder of JPEG Trading, a cryptocurrency trading firm that closely tracked the hack to monitor market conditions. Zoom in : Binance limited withdrawals and platforms including Tether and Circle froze more than $1 billion in cryptocurrencies, per Zhao. Such a step that would limit the scope of customer losses. Zhao and a Binance spokesperson said user funds are safe. The Binance spokesperson said the exchange's security teams are "reviewing all relevant information with urgency." The big picture: If estimates hold up, the suspected Binance hack would be the biggest crypto attack in history. In 2025, North Korea-linked hackers stole about $1.5 billion worth of crypto from the Bybit exchange. The country has turned hacking and scams into an industrial-scale scourge, focusing on crypto heists and a widespread practice of tricking Western companies into hiring North Korean workers . Between the lines : Crypto is a relatively common hacking target, but massive attacks can leave smaller exchanges vulnerable to collapse due to the potential for panicked withdrawals. Binance's size makes it more insulated, March said. "If this happened to any other business in crypto other than Binance, it would've been catastrophic." The exchange is capable of covering potential losses through its insurance and balance sheet, he said, although broad reverberations in crypto markets and prices remain possible. The intrigue: Reports of a breach came just hours after Polymarket confirmed it was facing a cyberattack, prompting the decentralized predictions market operator to pause trading for an hour after an attacker made off with at least $2.7 million in user funds. Researchers at Hudson Rock tied the Polymarket incident to a breach involving third-party website monitoring tool DebugBear , which said earlier Thursday it was responding to its own security incident. What to watch: Binance has yet to confirm who may be behind the attack and the total value of the currencies suspected hackers made off with.

9f8728e73761.text: Democrats' main Senate super PAC is privately telling top donors that Texas offers their best shot at flipping a deep-red Senate seat, followed by Ohio, where the race remains close. Senate Majority PAC also sees victories in Iowa and Alaska as within reach, though the outcomes could take longer to become clear. Why it matters: Democrats are increasingly confident about Election Day on Tuesday — and sharing their qualified optimism with their biggest donors. To retake the Senate, Democrats need to win two of those four states — all of which Trump won by double digits in 2024 — flip North Carolina and Maine, and avoid an upset in Michigan. JB Poersch, president of Senate Majority PAC, projected confidence that Democrats will wrest control of the Senate from Republicans during a private donor briefing this week as he walked through the races state by state. He also reminded donors that Kansas, where even Republicans are deeply worried, is a state Trump won by roughly 16 points in 2024. But it's in play . What they're saying: "This matches what we've been saying publicly and privately for weeks. There are signs of optimism in Texas, but it remains a toss-up, as do Iowa, Ohio and Alaska," said Lauren French, a spokesperson for SMP. "There is positive movement for Democrats, but it is critical to remember that every seat on the battleground map voted for Donald Trump by double digits," she said. "These are deep red states and we're focused on bringing them over the finish line so the Senate can work to provide real relief to families who are being crushed by the cost-of-living crisis." The big picture: Texas hasn't elected a Democratic senator since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988. Democrats thought they'd end the drought in 2018 and let themselves fall for then-Rep. Beto O'Rourke, who lost to Sen. Ted Cruz by 2.6 percentage points. Four years later, O'Rourke tried again to prove a Democrat could win statewide in Texas. He lost the governor's race by nearly 11 percentage points. This time around, Democrats have state Rep. James Talarico, who's narrowly led recent polls against Republican nominee Ken Paxton. Zoom in: During this unseasonably sunny week in Washington, private polls and scraps of data are flying from phone to phone at outdoor cafes as both parties search for a story to tell themselves, their candidates and their donors. At every table, there are essentially two camps: The pessimists find reasons to dismiss every glimmer of hope. Republicans are worried about a "red scream." The optimists blow past inconvenient facts that might kill their victory vibes. Some Democrats are "nauseously optimistic." In reality, optimists and pessimists — in both parties — are flying without instruments. Internal polls contradict each other by a point or three, door-knocking data is noisy, and early-vote numbers can be spun to tell almost any story. The bottom line: On some level, big-dollar donors know they lack the omniscience to read the political landscape with the same clarity they once brought to an IPO's S-1 filing. But they also believe they deserve better data and analysis than what's publicly available. At the very least, they want private briefings to give them a clearer picture than is epistemologically possible. Hence the flurry of briefings. The challenge for the super PACs is to return all the calls — and give donors hope without making promises they can't keep.

4f6272861312.text: By — Dante Chinni, The Conversation Dante Chinni, The Conversation By — Ari Pinkus, The Conversation Ari Pinkus, The Conversation Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/new-survey-finds-more-than-two-thirds-of-americans-believe-their-country-is-in-decline Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter New survey finds more than two-thirds of Americans believe their country is in decline Nation Oct 29, 2026 7:37 PM EDT This article originally appeared on The Conversation. Inflation is causing real economic pain. Worries about healthcare costs have jumped sharply. And 7 in 10 Americans believe the country is in decline. That is the landscape for the 2026 midterm election, according to a new survey from the American Communities Project at Michigan State University, which I direct. READ MORE: What our final poll before Election Day says about midterms and Trump The findings, which follow up previous data work the American Communities Project has done in 2023, 2024 and 2025, come from a survey of 2,155 American adults over two weeks in September 2026, conducted by the survey research firm SSRS, using an online panel and telephone, with a margin of error of +/- 2.4 percentage points. The American Communities Project studies 15 types of communities. Taken as a whole, the national numbers reveal an electorate that is unsettled, gloomy and likely looking for change. Inflation: Deepening concern Cost of living is a unifying concern for all Americans. For the past four years, when given a list of 20 issues – including abortion, climate change, gun violence, drug addiction, education, healthcare, housing, immigration and taxes – respondents have consistently reported that inflation is the No. 1 issue in their community. But the new data shows something more significant. Almost half of Americans, 47%, say they are experiencing real pain from rising prices – a sharp rise from previous years. In 2023, 2025 and 2026, we asked respondents whether they were experiencing "serious financial problems" due to price increases. In July 2023, 27% answered yes. In 2025, 30% said yes. In 2026, 47% said yes. This significant swing underscores that many Americans across the country are really hurting in this economy. For some groups, concern about costs reached well above 50%. For those ages 18-29 – members of Gen Z – 61% said they are dealing with serious financial problems because of price increases, the highest percentage among the four generational cohorts, including ages 30-49, 50-64 and 65+. Cost of living was also a particular concern reported among people of color. Overall, 65% of Hispanics and 63% of Black Americans said they are experiencing serious financial problems because of price increases. Healthcare: A rising issue Healthcare emerged as a top issue in our new survey. In 2025, 20% of respondents said it was a top concern in their community. This year, 30% cited healthcare as a top concern, a 10-point jump. That shift also made healthcare the No. 2 issue in this survey, after inflation. For some demographic groups, concern about healthcare in their community reached above one-third of respondents. Among those whose income falls between US$75,000 and $99,999, 36% said healthcare is a top issue; among Black Americans, 35% said so. This tracks with the policy changes and public health challenges since our 2025 survey. Many have lost health insurance, hospitals have closed, and disease outbreaks have affected communities. It also may be tied to increasing costs overall. The pain people feel from inflation in healthcare can be especially acute because the dollar amounts can be large. The United States in decline The 2026 survey data also showed a 15-point jump in the percentage of Americans who agree with the statement: The United States is in decline. The number is at 70% this year, up from 55% in 2025. In some ways that number makes sense. Consider the other numbers mentioned here – pain from inflation and concerns about healthcare – and the mood of Americans in general. READ MORE: Americans' opinion of economy drops to lowest level since 2014 But there is another important point in the data. That number, 70%, is exactly what it was in 2023, the first year the American Communities Project did a survey. In 2025, the "decline" number dropped to 55%, and that change was largely driven by communities that voted for President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. It was a measure of hope for the future, and it showed in massive improvements in the general hopefulness in communities such as the evangelical hubs, concentrated heavily in the South, rural middle America and the middle suburbs. The fact that the "decline" number is back to 70% suggests those same Trump-supporting communities have seen their hopes take a hit – and a deeper analysis of the data on the American Communities Project website shows just that. At the very least, the data suggests a very disillusioned electorate. Times and attitudes change It's important to keep the 2024 election in mind as the 2026 midterm elections near. It's a sign of how opinions and attitudes can change – and quickly. The data here represents this moment in time, and it will likely move after November, which is why we will field this same survey again after the new Congress is seated. On Oct. 26 we released our more detailed community-level findings on the American Communities Project website. A golden eagle chick has become the first to fledge from a nest on a managed grouse moor in the south of Scotland.
The bird - Beaky Junior - hatched in a nest in a secret location in the Moffat Hills, at a site used for recreational gamebird shooting.
It comes after a Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) report revealed that two-thirds of UK persecution incidents involving birds of prey had occurred at similar sites.
And it is being considered a "hugely significant milestone" by those running a project to boost golden eagle numbers in the region.
Dr Cat Barlow, chief executive of Restoring Upland Nature (Run) which is behind the scheme, said they had received "incredible support" from landowners and gamekeepers.
The project to relocate birds from the Highlands to a secret location in the Moffat Hills started in the summer of 2018.
Numbers in the south of Scotland had fallen to a handful of breeding pairs but they are now at a record level of more than 50 - despite some setbacks.
Birds have been shot at or killed and that is why the birth of Beaky Junior - one of five golden eagle chicks successfully fledged in the area this year - is being seen as so significant, since it happened on a managed grouse moor.
Earlier this year, the RSPB report highlighted 182 confirmed persecution incidents involving birds of prey in Scotland over a 10-year period.
It said they were widely scattered across the country but the majority - 64.3% - had occurred on land managed for gamebird shooting.
Against that backdrop, the efforts in southern Scotland to encourage estates and conservationists to work together are seen as particularly important.
Beaky Junior was even named by local gamekeepers in recognition of the "key role" they have played in helping golden eagles thrive.
Barlow explained: "It is wonderful to see a golden eagle hatch, fledge and fly freely from the newly-established nest of a translocated golden eagle that has made its home on a managed grouse moor in the Southern Uplands.
"This reflects the incredible support we have had from landowners and gamekeepers â from translocations in the Highlands, to continued monitoring and protection of birds and eyries on their lands and estates.
"Indeed their support has been absolutely vital to our success in restoring the population of golden eagles to record numbers."
She said the fledging of five chicks from the nests of birds they had translocated to southern Scotland was a "hugely significant milestone".
Barlow added that it gave "genuine hope" in the battle to reverse biodiversity decline and ensure future generations across Scotland, England and Wales could experience the "incredible sense of awe" when seeing a golden eagle.
Michael Clarke, who chairs Run, said individuals from "all walks of life" had helped the birds to thrive.
He added that they would continue to monitor the impact of the golden eagles on the area "with support of land managers, gamekeepers, farmers and the wider community".
The chief executive of landowner body Scottish Land and Estates, Sarah-Jane Laing, said it was thrilled to hear gamekeepers had named the chick.
"Beaky Junior's arrival serves as a powerful example of what can be achieved when land managers and conservationists unite behind a shared vision, grounded in trust and genuine partnership," she said.
"Seeing this magnificent species return to and flourish in these landscapes is something we can all take pride in."
The gamekeepers involved asked to remain anonymous in order to protect the location of the bird.
Speaking on their behalf, Mark Ewart, regional co-ordinator at the Southern Uplands Moorlands Group, added: "It is incredibly rewarding to see gamekeepers celebrated for the important role they have played in the success of Run's South of Scotland Golden Eagle Project.
"Monitoring and providing the right habitats for golden eagles and other species to flourish is an important part of what gamekeepers do on a day-to-day basis.
"To encounter golden eagles daily is the ultimate indicator of the success of the project-gamekeeper partnership."

be4c9200ec5b.text: By — Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-denies-federal-request-to-segregate-california-ballots-says-it-would-wreak-havoc-on-voting Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge denies federal request to segregate California ballots, says it would 'wreak havoc' on voting Politics Oct 29, 2026 6:57 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — A federal judge rejected on Wednesday a Trump administration request to stop California from processing the ballots of up to 20,000 people over allegations they are likely noncitizens, warning it would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections. READ MORE: California election officials frustrated, rattled by DOJ demand to sequester 'noncitizen' ballots The ruling by U.S. District Judge David O. Carter comes as more than 3.7 million people have already voted in the state. "Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable. Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred," Carter wrote. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process." Prosecutors for the Justice Department said they would immediately appeal the decision. The decision is the latest legal setback for President Donald Trump in his efforts to expand federal control over state-run elections ahead of voting that will decide control of Congress for the rest of his term. The Republican administration sued election officials in the Democratic state in mid-October, accusing the officials of failing to meet a 48-hour deadline to review a list of 20,000 people it alleged were likely noncitizens on the state's voter rolls. The administration had asked the judge to require the state to wait to count those ballots until the voters' immigration status could be verified. The Justice Department made a similar request in Washington state this week for the state to sequester ballots submitted by hundreds of people it suspects are not U.S. citizens. Meanwhile, another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent running for U.S. Senate doesn't win. All three states have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in Congress. Judge says Justice Department's request violates civil rights laws Carter's order was a forceful rebuke of the federal government's demand, arguing that segregating ballots at this time in the election would require counties to develop new methods for sorting ballots and "risk disenfranchising an untold number of voters." In other words, Carter argued, it would have the same effect as purging voters and therefore violates the National Voting Rights Act, which prohibits changes to voter rolls within 90 days of an election. The federal government's request, Carter wrote, "would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens." California mails ballots to all 23 million registered voters. Court filings show over 500,000 ballots had already been processed by this week, meaning their envelopes had been verified and the ballots removed. That would make it virtually impossible to know which ballot belonged to a particular voter, Los Angeles county officials have testified. Carter, an appointee of former Democratic President Bill Clinton, also rejected the Justice Department's argument that California was impeding the federal government's ability to enforce the law. He argued that prosecutors already demonstrated the ability to enforce election law when they arrested 28 noncitizens who had allegedly voted or registered to vote illegally. Carter previously said in court that he was inclined to appoint a special master to vet the government's data processes. His Wednesday order appeared to reverse course, and he did not establish one in his order denying the Trump administration's demands. Justice Department will appeal decision The federal government said it would file an appeal in the case for the second time on Wednesday evening. The USA's first appeal was denied by the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, since it preempted the district court's decision. Two of the three judges also expressed overwhelming skepticism about the merits of the lawsuit itself. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli doubled down on the lawsuit's arguments Wednesday. "Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials," Essayli wrote on social media following the ruling. "This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution." Essayli, who argued on behalf of the federal government on Tuesday, has previously said the federal government's request wouldn't impede the election. Instead, he argued that the Justice Department was trying to prevent the "dilution" of the vote with noncitizen voters. "Segregating a ballot does not prevent it from being counted later," Essayli said. "It is designed to preserve the status quo and prevent the infection of our election with illegal ballots." California's decision echoes national trend Election law experts following the case have said the ruling is consistent with a broader change. David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, said the district court's ruling "confirmed what we already know: states, not the federal government, run elections." He said the DOJ's demands of California election officials, so close to Election Day, seemed "designed to cause chaos." 5c1351a0b711.text: By — Deema Zein Deema Zein By — Bryan Gallion Bryan Gallion Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-how-does-the-associated-press-call-2026-midterm-election-winners-4-things-to-know Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: How does The Associated Press call 2026 midterm election winners? 4 things to know Politics Oct 29, 2026 6:55 PM EDT The Associated Press has tracked voting in U.S. elections for 178 years, and it's gearing up to make thousands more race calls in midterm contests this Election Day. Watch the video in the player above. Along with gathering ballot returns to declare winners, for the first time in a major general election the AP is now partnering with broadcast news networks to survey the electorate for the new Voter Poll. This questionnaire is an updated way to analyze voter demographics and motivations, and it will offer results in every state where there's a statewide election. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Here's how the AP's election processes work. How does the AP know ballots are counted? The AP will tabulate results for nearly 7,000 races, including national congressional contests, state legislative and gubernatorial races, as well as some local elections for mayor, city council and school board, according to David Scott, the AP's vice president for U.S. election services. About 4,000 journalists working for the AP will collect results from local voting precincts and election offices across the country. Around 1,000 vote-entry clerks will answer calls from those AP workers to enter candidates' vote totals into the news agency's election night reporting system. READ MORE: A guide to the key ballot measures voters will decide on Election Day That data is matched to election returns posted on county and state websites or delivered by electronic feeds to ensure accuracy. The AP's Decision Team then analyzes those results to determine who won. "We like to say that what we do at AP on election night is the single largest act of journalism there is," Scott said. How and when people vote has changed over time, and the AP's data collection has followed suit. Back in 1972, Scott said, about 95% of Americans voted at a polling place on Election Day, compared to less than half of Americans now. Most people are casting their ballots before Election Day, by mail or through in-person early voting. How does the AP call election winners? The AP's Decision Team is comprised of journalists, data analysts and political science experts who study elections full-time. A race won't be called until a candidate has reached the point where competitors no longer have a path to victory. "Not until that moment," Scott said. "Our certainty is our standard." WATCH: 2026 midterms preview, plus your questions on voting Many races are called on election night, but some take longer. The AP called the 2020 presidential election for Joe Biden four days later, for example. And it didn't call the 2000 race between George W. Bush and Al Gore, sticking by its assessment that the margin in Florida was too close to declare a winner. Out of more than 11,000 races in which the AP declared winners during this year's primary elections, Scott said his team made three mistakes, citing incorrect information from election officials and a technical issue. What is The Voter Poll and what does it tell us? The Voter Poll will interview voters in person about whom they voted for and what issues mattered to them when they cast their ballots on Election Day, similar to traditional exit polls. But the survey is also interviewing people who voted early — reaching them online, by phone or by mail. The AP used its own system, AP VoteCast, to gather insights about the vote in general elections from 2018 to 2024. It partnered with ABC News, CBS News, CNN, Fox News, MS NOW and NBC News last year to develop this new poll, and the broadcast networks will join in conducting the research this year. READ MORE: What our final poll before Election Day says about midterms and Trump About 75,000 voters are being surveyed before Election Day, and around 25,000 more will be interviewed at polling places in 15 states on Nov. 3. The survey will also analyze the demographics of states and of their electorates to see how they align. While races can't be called from this data, it can provide a sense of what direction an election could be going. Scott said voter demographic shifts in 2024 "pointed early in the night to success" for Trump. The rise in voting ahead of Election Day led to this updated survey method. "Really what we've tried to do with our colleagues at the broadcast networks is design a methodology that reaches Americans, no matter how you cast your ballot," Scott said. "You have the opportunity for us to ask you questions so we can understand the fullness of the American electorate." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. b44390618601.text: U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of forces in the Middle East, briefed President Trump Thursday on the state of the Iran war, with a focus on the ongoing naval blockade , according to two U.S. officials. Why it matters: As he did before Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 and Operation Epic Fury in February, Trump is pursuing dual tracks — trying to reach a deal to restart peace talks while also preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations after the midterms. Behind the scenes: Trump wanted to hear directly from the CENTCOM head on whether the naval blockade is working, the U.S. officials said. Cooper also briefed Trump on the military operation for guiding oil tankers out of the Strait of Hormuz to global energy markets. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, White House envoy Steve Witkoff and other senior officials also attended the meeting, the officials said. The White House and CENTCOM declined to comment. The Wall Street Journal first reported the meeting. Driving the news: A group of regional mediators led by Qatar is trying to get the U.S. and Iran to head off a resumption of war after the midterms in favor of negotiations. Qatari mediators recently delivered a letter from Vice President Vance to Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Gen. Mohsen Rezaei. Vance proposed restarting negotiations but stressed that any talks would have to address Iran's nuclear program. Trump and Vance met Wednesday to discuss a possible gesture of goodwill toward Iran, such as sending humanitarian goods like food and medicine, according to a source with knowledge. What they're saying: U.S. Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack told CNN on Thursday that the U.S. and Iran are "very close" to a deal to deescalate tensions. "I think we're very close to finally getting to a place where we can say, 'Let's just have a timeout,'" he said. "We're not going to have an overall solution immediately, but we can allow the region to find its own pace." The other side: Iranian officials on Thursday continued to demand the U.S. take a series of steps — such as lifting the blockade, releasing Iranian frozen funds and allowing Iran to sell oil — before resuming negotiations on their nuclear program.

d20c526d9b5e.text: By — Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/doordash-offers-17-billion-for-instacart-in-what-would-be-big-grocery-delivery-consolidation Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter DoorDash offers $17 billion for Instacart in what would be big grocery delivery consolidation Economy Oct 29, 2026 6:41 PM EDT DoorDash is offering $17 billion to buy Instacart in a deal that could consolidate the grocery delivery business in the U.S. and abroad. The companies say the tie-up would combine DoorDash's global reach and expertise in logistics with Instacart's purpose-built technology and long relationships with grocers. It could also help the companies better compete with rivals like Amazon. READ MORE: Instacart ends program where users see different prices for the same item at same store But it could also lead to less competition in the delivery space, which could raise prices for consumers and give grocers fewer partners to negotiate with. "They were competing for a share of consumers' wallet," said Randall Sargent, a partner specializing in grocery and retail at the consulting firm Oliver Wyman. "As a general economic principle, less competition and more consolidation tends to be worse for consumers." The deal is expected to be finalized by the end of 2027 or in early 2028 if it's approved by Instacart shareholders and government regulators. Instacart's name and app will remain Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app would remain, and Instacart's 600,000 shoppers — who are independent contractors — would be able to continue fulfilling orders as before. Consumers who are currently paying $9.99 per month for separate DashPass and Instacart+ memberships, which give them free delivery on most orders and other perks, would be able to pay one fee instead of two, DoorDash said. Instacart customers would also have access to 50,000 additional stores that are on DoorDash's platform. Grocers would also be able to choose either delivery platform. Tony Xu, DoorDash's co-founder and CEO, said the deal could help local grocers compete with larger players. Walmart is the largest U.S. grocer, with 21% share of spending, followed by Costco and Amazon, which each have 8% share, according to Numerator, a market research company. "Over the past decade or even two decades, what you see is the largest companies are only eating more and more of the pie. Why is that? It's because they've invested aggressively into capabilities like a modern technology stack, like fast delivery, like new fulfillment models," Xu said Thursday during a conference call with investors. "That's what this combination is really about, where DoorDash and Instacart can give every retailer a fighting chance at competing in the modern-day era." The deal would also help DoorDash and Instacart fend off rivals like Walmart, which has been moving into restaurant delivery. Walmart partnered with Subway, its largest in-store restaurant tenant, this past summer and has since expanded to select locations at Dunkin' and Papa Johns. The company said it now has 2,400 restaurant locations on its restaurant delivery platform. DoorDash has been growing its grocery business DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food, electronics and many other products. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. That dwarfs Instacart, which fulfilled 338 million orders last year. DoorDash has a market value of $73 billion. DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. Kroger partnered with the San Francisco company in 2022 but initially allowed the company to deliver only flowers, sushi and prepared meals from a limited number of stores. The partnership expanded last fall, and DoorDash now lists the full inventory of all 2,700 U.S. Kroger stores in its online marketplace. DoorDash scored another coup last month when it added delivery from Costco. DoorDash's move into grocery has hurt Instacart. Five years ago, Instacart commanded 26% of spending on U.S. delivery platforms; that share has fallen to 18%, according to Consumer Edge, a market research company. DoorDash's share grew from 44% to 59% in that same period. Uber Eats' share held steady at just under 20%. Combined company could attract more ads, but also scrutiny Sargent said a combined DoorDash and Instacart could potentially attract more ad revenue from food companies. Right now, Instacart can only share what consumers put in their baskets, for example, but a combined company could also show them what customers ordered for takeout lunch. "Food companies want to spread their ad dollars around and reach customers efficiently," Sargent said. "The more you can hand them an audience that you know all about, the more formidable a challenger this new company is." But the tie-up will also be subject to scrutiny from antitrust regulators in the U.S. and elsewhere, particularly at a time when consumers are agitated about food price inflation. Ethan Litwin, an antitrust attorney and partner with New York-based Shinder Cantor Lerner, said it could be problematic if DoorDash controls Instacart's technology, since many grocers use that technology to power their online storefronts. "DoorDash could therefore cut rivals off, outmatch them on targeting and logistics, or monitor competitors' pricing and discounting in real time, which could facilitate coordination on pricing," Litwin said. "I expect that the parties will call these efficiencies, but an advantage big enough to build a monopoly will not stay consumer-friendly for long." Acquisition was discussed for a while Apoorva Mehta

81a0adef426b.text: As candidates make a final push to win over voters ahead of Election Day, Lisa Desjardins takes a deep dive into the battle for the House of Representatives. Where does it all stand? Lisa Desjardins: Expensive and expansive. Look at this map of all the races. These are the 81 somewhat to very competitive races that we are tracking. Now, The Cook Political Report lists a lot of competitive races. It's important to also know this number, three. This is the magic number. Democrats need to flip three seats on net in order to take over the House. So I don't want to just look at this large map, but let's look at the most competitive seats that are toss-ups or leans. These 50 dots represent those 50 seats that may determine the fate of the House of Representatives. What's important here is who occupies them now. Look at this. It's mostly Republicans, 39 of these seats occupied by Republicans. They are on defense. Remember that magic number three? So, essentially Democrats need to pick up three seats right here -- this is the line -- in order to flip the House. Now, The Cook Political Report already forecasts that Democrats are likely to flip some seats. How many? Ten. So, if you remember this line that determines control of the House, Democrats have already put themselves in position to pass that. And, right now, Republicans need to push back. But they are in a good position at this moment, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: And on the substance of all these races, the economy is the top issue, per usual. But how and where is that playing out? Lisa Desjardins: Right. I love looking at this the substance. Let's talk first of all, about housing, that issue that we found in Northeastern Pennsylvania. These are the places where housing is particularly an issue in the campaign. You see it in Florida, in Nevada, in Southern California. But let's talk about the issue that a lot of Americans also feel, gas and fuel prices. It is everywhere, but I want to point out these races where they are particularly facing record high fuel prices, or like in Maine or Alaska, where they are more dependent on diesel or heating oil. And let's focus on one race in particular where this is a factor. Let's go to Colorado's Eighth District. This is a situation where the gas prices have still been rising this month. The Democrat, Manny Rutinel, says that the issue is Iran and tariffs. He says he had pushed back against President Trump. But the Republican, Gabe Evans, says, no, it's the problem of regulation, and he has supported President Trump. So this is a factor in this race. Geoff Bennett: And what about the other issues driving these midterm races? Lisa Desjardins: There's one more I want to talk about because a lot of the country is, and that is data centers. Here's an example of four of the races where that has become a campaign issue this year. And I want to focus on one. This is Central Michigan, Michigan's Seventh District. The Democrat, Will Lawrence, won his primary in part because he campaigned so hard on a ban, at least temporarily, on data centers. This is a district where we just saw a $10 billion data center put on hold because of protests from locals. Now, Tom Barrett, the Republican incumbent, he has a different tact. He instead says each locality should be able to decide whether they want the data center or not. This race is a good test of how far voters want to go when it comes to data centers. And all of these issues, of course, around the country do have ties to the economy. And it's important to see how that layers in. Geoff Bennett: Lisa Desjardins, our thanks to you, as always. Lisa Desjardins: You're welcome.

cfbfc7ba37d7.text: Israel is facing political uncertainty after an election that produced no clear governing majority. But what do the results reveal about how Israelis want leaders to confront the country's challenges? Nick Schifrin discussed that with Tamir Hayman, former chief of Israeli military intelligence and current executive director of the Institute for National Security Studies. Geoff Bennett: Israel is once again facing political uncertainty after an election that has produced no clear governing majority amid competing allegations of voting fraud and irregularities. But beyond the political maneuvering, what do the results reveal about how Israelis want their leaders to confront the country's mounting challenges? For that, our Nick Schifrin spoke with retired Major General Tamir Hayman, former chief of Israeli military intelligence and current executive director of the Institute for National Security Studies. That's a leading Israeli think tank. Nick Schifrin: Tamir Hayman, thank you very much. Welcome to the "News Hour." Regardless of whether Benjamin Netanyahu stays prime minister or Gadi Eisenkot becomes prime minister, is there an overall agreement on how Israel should approach its national security since October the 7th? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): It seems like Israelis are still in the trauma after post-October 7, and they are reluctant on going to any kinds of concessions in the Palestinian-Israeli conflict. Most parties argue for a very hawkish, proactive approach in terms of the next state needed in confronting Hamas and Iran, et cetera, et cetera. So it seems like, in that aspect there's a proactive, hawkish military, security approach that is accepted, and we are not entering a zone of agreements or a peace-aspiring environment. Nick Schifrin: You write that pursuing peace is considered a danger, and -- quote -- "War is necessary and preventive war is preferable." Does that mean Israel is set to be in a perpetual state of war? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): Let me just emphasize that, in this article, I wanted to provoke a discussion, so I exaggerated a little bit in order to be able to observe trends. But it seems to be describing trends that are in the consensus. Nick Schifrin: And where Israel is going? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): And where Israel going, if not diverted. We are headed right now, brings us into very dangerous place. Nick Schifrin: Does Israeli leadership believe that a perpetual state of war is better? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): They do not believe that peace is a viable or tangible solution right now. Most Israelis will consider any form of a peace as weakness, naive approach, trusting the Arabs, trusting the enemies. The general sentiment is, we trusted the Arabs, and they betrayed us. So what left is an ongoing state of confrontation. Nick Schifrin: You describe, even if it's exaggerated, this severing with the United States. And, again, I will I will read it, knowing that you say it's exaggerated, but it's very provocative. "The United States is a declining power, and, given its ongoing social and political shifts, will soon abandon Israel. In any event, excessive dependence on the U.S. exposes Israel to the influence of a progressive American value system incompatible with Israel's Jewish character." I mean, it's an understatement to call that controversial among American Jews, but is that where we're headed? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): It seems like we are losing our position as a consensus among Americans, and we are losing the bipartisan approach. We have already lost the bipartisan position, and we are going to be maybe homeless in the political spectrum of United States. Secondly, the fact that we are dependent on our national security on capabilities and backing from United States create vulnerabilities. So, what is the rational outcome? We must rely on ourselves. Nick Schifrin: Netanyahu has referred to Israel as super Sparta, basically being self-reliant on weapons, as you have been describing. He's even suggested that Israel might have to rely on Bitcoin because of future sanctions. How isolated, in your opinion, is Israel? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): The idea that if Israel will be ever isolated, it is an existential threat to the existence of Israel, OK? The economy is based on high-tech and an advanced science. That cannot be established in an isolation mode based on crypto. Second, there's a true threat of isolation and sanctions. But the way to handle it is to approach the causes of that. Nick Schifrin: But given the results of this election, even if we don't know exactly the numbers, in which Netanyahu and his bloc maintained the lead over the opposition bloc, doesn't that suggest that these trends are accelerating, that many Israelis have embraced these ideas that you're critiquing? Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): The political spectrum map is moving right. The problem is that there is radicalization in the right-wing establishment after October 7. Nick Schifrin: And back to the concept that you write about. And again, acknowledging that you say that you're exaggerating, there's one fundamental conclusion that you have, and that it's that the consensus is to -- quote -- "guarantee Israel's continued existence as a Jewish state, even at the cost of eroding its democratic values." Explain that in simple terms. Maj. Gen. Tamir Hayman (Res.): The whole article asks critical question, whether it's good for Israel to move in that path. Of course, it is wrong. And that's what -- that's the whole purpose of this idea. Why do I emphasize the tension between democratic and Jewish values? Because if we're not going to do anything in the Palestinian arena, and we will annex the Palestinian territories, we will annex the West Bank into Israel, we will not have a Jewish majority. And the only way to maintain a Jewish statehood is by eroding democracy. This is an, again, existential threat to the identity of Israel as a Jewish democratic state

In less than two weeks, U.S. Senate leaders plan to take an initial vote on the divisive permitting reform bill aimed at easing regulatory barriers that can delay energy projects. As the date nears, some of the country’s leading environmental groups are ramping up their opposition, arguing that the measure would do more harm than good.
A new report from Resources for the Future, a research nonprofit, projects that the bill’s power-sector provisions would cut carbon emissions by 1.8 gigatons by 2041 and reduce annual electricity-system costs by an average of 3.5 percent to 7 percent compared to a scenario without the bill.
But the projected benefits are unlikely to convince the bill’s critics, partly because the analysis doesn’t address the provisions that have drawn the most opposition, including changes to the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
The debate over the bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, has divided environmental and clean energy advocates and threatens to unravel a compromise between the bill’s Democratic and Republican co-sponsors.
On one side, clean energy business groups and advocacy organizations praise the bill’s approach to accelerating timelines for building transmission lines and renewable energy projects. On the other side, key environmental advocacy groups say the proposal would speed up fossil fuel infrastructure buildout and remove current tools to oppose projects.
“Over the next two years, BAAJA would create more legal runway for this president to make corrupt deals and greenlight harmful projects of all kinds, and it would constrain any future president from repairing the damage,” said Abigail Dillen, president of Earthjustice, an environmental law nonprofit, in a commentary posted on Tuesday.
The same day, four Senate Democrats sent a letter to the bill’s co-sponsors saying they have concerns that President Donald Trump’s administration cannot be trusted to follow through on promises that were made during negotiations.
“Beyond consideration of the actual text, the promise of BAAJA will only succeed if President Trump takes care that it is faithfully executed,” reads the letter from Democratic Sens. Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, Ed Markey of Massachusetts and Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden, both of Oregon. “The Trump administration’s record gives us no basis to assume that he will.”
The senators cite the Trump administration’s cancellation of already-approved clean energy grants and loans and evidence that decisions were made with intent to harm states that voted for Democrats. They said the administration should reinstate all canceled awards and commit in writing to no longer basing grant decisions on the political affiliation of a state’s elected officials.
If the administration doesn’t comply, the senators have threatened to oppose a motion to proceed to debate on the bill at a vote scheduled for Nov. 9. Losing the support of four senators who have been vocal advocates for environmental protection could make it harder to secure the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster.
In a statement, a Trump administration spokesperson said the White House supports the bill because it will deliver jobs and investment.
“The text of the legislation has been published, and all that is left to do is vote,” the spokesperson said. “We are in direct conversations with the lead negotiators in the Senate and are looking forward to action on this historic legislation to unleash more energy in the United States.”
A co-sponsor of the bill, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-Rhode Island, has also expressed concerns that the Trump administration will go to extraordinary lengths to oppose renewable energy even if the bill becomes law.
“We await real signs of regulatory good faith,” he said in a post on X, along with a link to a Bloomberg article about the administration’s recent contradictory actions on wind power.
Meanwhile, a coalition of conservative groups, many funded by the petrochemical billionaire Koch family’s network, urged the Senate this week to pass the bill to “protect property rights, promote energy abundance, and restore America’s ability to build.”
Emissions Cuts, But an Incomplete Picture
The new analysis by Resources for the Future follows several by other organizations that also show substantial cuts in emissions resulting from the power-sector provisions of the bill.
Resources for the Future is a leader using economic models to estimate the effects of complex legislation. Among the findings:
- The bill would increase the country’s transmission line capacity by 30 percent by 2041, meaning more power can be transported on interstate power lines. A lack of transmission capacity is one of the main factors impeding construction of new wind, solar and battery projects and more lines would allow more of those systems to be built.
- Building new, cleaner power sources would help displace some of the older, more polluting sources on the grid, adding 60 gigawatts of clean power capacity compared with a baseline scenario without the bill. The analysis also found that removing existing constraints would lead to a small increase in combined-cycle natural gas plants, though that effect would diminish over time.
- Power-sector carbon dioxide emissions would be lower under the bill than without the bill, although both scenarios show emissions growth over the study period. Adopting the bill would reduce cumulative carbon emissions by 1.83 gigatons through 2041. In the final year, emissions would be 6 percent less than the baseline level.
