In a new book, Ressa warns of other threats to those same freedoms. Amna Nawaz spoke with Ressa about “The Fight Back." Geoff Bennett: Journalist and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa chronicled her fight against the Duterte regime in the Philippines in her 2022 book, ""How to Stand Up to a Dictator." She detailed years of attacks in her reporting and her newsroom's struggle to defend press freedom and democracy. Now, in a new book, Ressa warns of different threats to those same freedoms. Amna Nawaz spoke with her earlier today. Amna Nawaz: According to Maria Ressa, there's a dual threat now by autocratic leaders and big tech companies weaponizing information and algorithms to create new crises for democracy and humanity. Thanks for having me, Amna. Amna Nawaz: You talk in the book about what you call an unholy alliance between state power and platform power. What do you mean by that? Maria Ressa: A decade of harms from artificial intelligence, right? We're only talking about the tail end of it. But we have talked a lot about my two dictators in the Philippines. And my second dictator, who I would argue is more powerful is Mark Zuckerberg, because, at that point, 93 percent of Filipinos on the Internet were on Facebook. Facebook is our Internet. And here's the part. They both act with impunity, but Rodrigo Duterte is now waiting at The Hague for his trial to begin, his charges of crimes against humanity, while, from 2016 to today, Mark Zuckerberg is still acting with impunity. Amna Nawaz: We have seen that battle for facts, battle for the truth play out here in the United States. As we talk here, we're days away from another critical midterm election. You break it down in the book to talk about the convergence of three crises, truth, order, and accountability. Maria Ressa: Yes. Amna Nawaz: How similar is all of this to what you saw under Duterte in the Philippines? And be specific to what we're seeing here in the U.S. now. Maria Ressa: What we lived through in the Philippines is that we found out we needed to leave the virtual world to come to the real world, right, and because I was getting an average of 98 messages per hour. When we came into the real world, that was how we had a whole-of-society approach that ultimately led to the arrest of Rodrigo Duterte. And then we had just recently Brazil. Brazil, if you remember, right, they have the same two dictators we had in the Philippines in 2016. President Trump, similar, right?The state and Meta, Mark Zuckerberg under a different name now. And what the -- after the first run-off elections, when it looked like President Lula was going to lose, I'd never sensed such a desperation in Brazilians. And they used WhatsApp to mobilize in the real world. And they mobilized the largest ever out, same thing that happened in Serbia. This time, the students, they moved from the virtual world to the real world. I don't see that same kind of desperation yet in America. But I do see an awareness that AI and, more importantly, data centers are something Americans don't want. And that seems to be bipartisan. But, having said that, this is the moment, right? The world is looking at America. What choices are you going to make? Amna Nawaz: You offer very specific, tangible steps at the end of each of your 10 chapters that you want people to try to follow just to be aware of the role that they play in the spread of misinformation... Maria Ressa: Yes. Amna Nawaz: ... in the maybe falling apart of accountability in many ways too. The very first chapter, step one, you say track your screen time for seven days. Maria Ressa: Yes, absolutely. Amna Nawaz: Why is that important for Americans to do? Maria Ressa: Because think about it. The more time you spend on here, the less time you spend in person with someone else. And this is not meant to educate you or to build real intimacy, real connections. This is done for power and profit. It's meant to keep you scrolling, right? And so that first step, how much of your life have you given to screens, to technology that is both extractive and predatory? And then the second step after that in chapter one is delete the app, one app on your phone, and hopefully it's the one that makes you angriest, because what the technology has done is to take the worst of us as people. And when you're angry, you stay scrolling the longest. So that gives more power and money to the tech company, but takes away from you, right? So that's -- these are the steps, 10 chapters, 10 steps at the end of every chapter. And at the end of it, I put 10 strategic goals to defend our rights, to protect our rights. But I had a debate with my publisher on this because they wanted me to put it in -- at the back cover of the book. I didn't want to do that because then you would look there first and you will look at it and you will say, oh, my God, that's like climbing Mount Everest. It isn't hard. And every step, one step at a time, I learned this in the Philippines. I think the other part is this. When you are the target, and each of us on these platforms are the t

HUNTSVILLE, Ala.—Candidates for Alabama’s second-highest office took the stage Wednesday for what was the first major-party debate for a statewide office since 2010, the year Republicans took the reins of government from Democrats for the first time in the modern era.
In a debate hosted by WHNT, a Huntsville-based television station, state Rep. Phillip Ensler, a Democrat, and former Republican Party Chairman John Wahl answered questions from moderators and engaged in significant back-and-forth for about an hour, including on a couple of environmental and energy issues.
One major sticking point in the debate was the impact of data centers on Alabamians, their communities and their energy bills.
Asked whether he believes data centers are good for Alabama, Wahl said he thinks the facilities are inevitable but that he shares the concerns of some residents about their impacts.
“Data centers are a necessary evil,” Wahl said. “We already have them. We all like our YouTube, our cloud, our streaming services. But the question is when these are moving into communities, we have to make sure that those communities are protected.”
The demand for data centers in Alabama and across the country has been driven largely by the spread of artificial intelligence tools like large language models, not by the use of services like YouTube or Netflix, according to experts. If built to full capacity, data center campuses proposed in Alabama would consume more energy than all of the homes in the state combined, an Inside Climate News analysis found.
“We want the capital investment,” Wahl said. “We need data centers, but we need to do it the right way.”
Ensler, the first statewide candidate to propose a moratorium on new data center construction, said he’s met with residents across the state who have made their views about the facilities clear.
“There are residents all over that are very concerned about the lack of transparency. They’re concerned about data centers being forced on their communities,” he said. “They’re concerned that Alabama Power is [jacking] up their prices.”
An Inside Climate News investigation found that Alabamians paid the highest average residential electricity bills in the nation in 2024, the latest year with complete data at the time.
Ensler has made data centers and concerns around Alabama Power, the state’s powerful electric utility, a focal point of his campaign. Ensler, from Montgomery, has visited Lowndes County, whose residents are fighting a proposed hyperscale data center, five times.
Hours before the debate, and in the days leading up to it, Ensler stood in solidarity with Fenn Church at his home in Shelby County. Church has been in a months-long legal dispute with Alabama Power over its use of eminent domain to lay transmission lines across his property.
“Alabama Power thinks they can just walk over anyone and everyone,” Ensler has said of the situation. “They’re just trying to flex their muscles and intimidate people, and if they can do that to him and do it here, they can do it anywhere.”
In a statement, a representative of Alabama Power said that the utility understands “that property is personal, and we remain committed to treating property owners fairly and respectfully.
“The Alabama Supreme Court’s decision allows work on this section of the transmission line to move forward, supporting a project that is an important investment in the security and reliability of the electric grid for the customers and communities we serve,” the emailed statement said.
Church had won a temporary victory against the utility in lower court earlier this year, receiving a preliminary injunction from a Circuit Court judge that prevented Alabama Power from accessing the property while the lawsuit moved forward.
Last Wednesday, the Alabama Supreme Court granted a motion from the utility to stay that decision. Since then, Fenn and the utility have been at a stalemate.

Church has said he’s attempted to have U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, the Republican candidate for governor, act as a mediator between himself and Alabama Power. But Ensler, Church said, is the only candidate who has come to his property to stand toe to toe with the utility.
“And I so appreciate him for it,” Church said. “It’s not about Republican or Democrat. It’s about what’s right.”
The topic of the Public Service Commission, the state’s utility regulator, arose at the debate when Wahl accused Ensler of supporting an effort to take away Alabamians’ right to vote for lieutenant governor by having the governor and lieutenant governor run as a ticket.
Alabama lieutenant governor is primarily charged with presiding over the state Senate. If the office of governor becomes vacant, the lieutenant governor assumes the state’s highest office.
Ensler and Doug Jones, the Democratic candidate for governor, have said they would support a state constitutional amendment that would have voters elect their governor and lieutenant governor on the same ticket, the method used by most states with both roles and similar to the way federal elections for president and vice president work.
“I think that’s a bad move,” Wahl said. “I don’t like it.”
Ensler responded that any changes like that would have to be approved by Alabama voters through a constitutional amendment. Ensler then brought up the Public Service Commission overhaul.
“Who has taken away the right to vote from people is Republicans who pushed a bill to change the Public Service Commission and take away people’s voices for a very important body at a time in which utility rates are going up,” Ensler said. “So if we’re concerned about taking away the voice of the people, that was done by Republicans when it comes to the Public Service Commission.”

b7e57a6b26be.text: Much of the debate over higher education today centers on cost, career prospects and whether a college degree can prepare students for a rapidly changing job market. But in an era increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, one of the oldest skills taught on college campuses may be more valuable than ever. Paul Solman reports for our higher education series, Rethinking College. Geoff Bennett: Much of the debate over higher education today centers on cost, career prospects, and whether a college degree can prepare students for a rapidly changing job market. But in an era increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence, one of the oldest skills taught on college campuses may be more valuable than ever. Paul Solman reports for the next installment in our higher education series, Rethinking College. Paul Solman: Isolated by COVID, bombarded by social media, screen-swamped in general, and headed for an all-bets-are-off job market, no wonder today's students feel, to use a lament from my college days, as if they're up a tree, that is, precariously perched. Well, most of us remember from college learning to fend for ourselves by making friends outside the safe bubble of home and high school. But nowadays, with all the job pressure today's students face, is learning to socialize still as crucial? Jill Barry: I think, for me, it is one of the most important aspects, because when you're in college, you're meeting all these people of different backgrounds and you want to be able to use that knowledge once you graduate into a job. Paul Solman: Is it the single most important aspect of college, learning to live on your own, be with other people? Kosi Chugbo-Junius: Yes, I think it is like the single most important. I think whether you're an engineer, whether you're a science person, business, anything, that's the one thing I think all -- any job you're looking for, anything you want to do beyond here is going to have in common. You're going to have to work with people. Paul Solman: For better or worse. Kosi Chugbo-Junius: For better or worse. (LAUGHTER) Paul Solman: We started this story last spring at Michigan universities, where the emphasis from the top was crystal clear, not so much socializing as reorienting college to get students jobs. Brendan Kelly, President, Eastern Michigan University: It's not about courses and credit hours anymore. And that's been our model for the last 100 years. Paul Solman: Eastern Michigan University President Brendan Kelly. Brendan Kelly: We have to understand that our business is rooted in the student, and then has to be connected to their participation in the economy after graduation. Paul Solman: Job readiness is equally top of mind for Michigan State President Kevin Guskiewicz. Kevin Guskiewicz, President, Michigan State University: We have got a ranking recently two years in a row as top 10 among all publics for employability. That's a metric that we're proud of and one that we advertise proudly. Paul Solman: But when we talk to students, they emphasize something different. Reilly Coon, Michigan State Graduate Student: I come from a rural community in Northern Wisconsin, and so going to college for me was the first exposure I'd had to new ideas, new people. It was the most diverse environment I was ever in. Paul Solman: Michigan State grad student Reilly Coon got her undergraduate degree at the University of Wisconsin. Reilly Coon: I'm sure three years from now I won't remember every single thing or every reading, but the skills gained from that are I think essential for going out into the world and have definitely made me a more holistic human being and just helped me develop as a person. Itzel Segovia, Michigan State Alumna: I came from Texas. And it's a very big Latino community, so when I came here, it was, like, very diverse. Paul Solman: We heard the same thing from new MSU Itzel Segovia. Itzel Segovia: So I met people from all different backgrounds, and I will catch myself, like, on a Tuesday morning eating pho because of the friend that I made, and she's from Vietnam. So I think that it's essential to create those relationships in college, because that's one thing that will go with you through life. Paul Solman: And we didn't just hear it in Michigan; 800 miles east at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, same story. Kosi Chugbo-Junius: I came here, I didn't know a single person. Paul Solman: Senior Kosi Chugbo-Junius. Kosi Chugbo-Junius: Everything I have here, every resource I lean on is someone that I had to form like a social connection with. Like, I rely on that every day. Paul Solman: Seniors Jill Barry and Ben Luu. Jill Barry: When you're in college, you kind of develop a sense of self and you become more yourself, and you know how to communicate with people, and you're more confident in who you are. Paul Solman: When you first came here, how freaked out were you about, say, meeting other kids or meeting girls? Ben Luu, Student, University of Massachusetts Amherst: Oh, I would say it was intimidating. But, as you get along, it gets easier. Like, now I'm an R.A. on campus, so I live in with a bunch of kids, and so it kind of builds on you. Like, when -- if you were to ask me in freshman year if I were to ever be an R.A., like, I would have never even dreamt of it. But as... Paul Solman: Would you have talked to me when you were a freshman if I came to you at a table? Ben Luu: Probably not. I would probably run away or something. I was a very shy kid in high school. Paul Solman: Shy, isolated. So many higher ed students these days actually report feeling lonely. Betsy Cracco, University of Massachusetts Amherst: We start to see the erosion of social skills because people are spending so much time in virtual world. So when they come to campus, it might be the first time they're really immersed in a community. Paul Solman: Betsy Cracco runs the student well-being initiative at UMass Amherst. More of a challenge now than it was? Betsy Cracco: M

618a213a121d.text: Tap the kegs and break out the bratwurst, the Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions! Milwaukee is the smallest market in the major leagues. But this year, the Brewers dominated the regular season, and then rolled through the playoffs with ruthless efficiency. To break it all down, Stephanie Sy spoke with Jason Gay, a sports columnist at The Wall Street Journal. Announcer: Two-one pitch, Palacios grounds one softly. Unshakable, unstoppable, and champions at last, the Milwaukee Brewers! (CHEERING) Geoff Bennett: Well, tap the kegs and break out the bratwurst. The Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions. The win is the first in the franchise's 58-year history. And, as Stephanie Sy tells us, it capped a campaign that was as improbable as it was inevitable -- Stephanie. Stephanie Sy: Yes, you can't forget the cheese curds, Geoff. Geoff Bennett: True. Stephanie Sy: The Brewers are the smallest market team in the Major Leagues, but this year they dominated the regular season and then rolled through the playoffs with ruthless efficiency, including an emphatic sweep of the defending champion Dodgers, a team with a payroll more than twice their size. To break it all down, we're joined now by Jason Gay, sports columnist at The Wall Street Journal. What a night for Milwaukee, right, Jason? I mean, you have called this World Series a triumph. And it has, of course, the irresistible makings of an underdog story with the Brewers outspent, but never outplayed this whole season. How did they do it? Jason Gay, The Wall Street Journal: They did it by reverting to some old-school baseball. They started playing what people know as small ball. They were running. They were hitting to opposite fields. They were even bunting. Bunting's really frowned upon in 2026. They could generate runs and they were relentless. You saw in this World Series, you saw against the Dodgers Milwaukee was never down and out. They were always coming back. This was a team really without a weakness. Their pitching was fantastic, and they were clutch all the way through. Stephanie Sy: And the series itself challenged the assumption that the highest paid players were necessarily going to always win, not only with the Dodgers being bested, but Tampa Bay beating the Yankees on their way through the World Series. What does that say to you? Jason Gay: It says that the high school Bullies were vanquished in the corridor before this World Series. I mean, you had two powerhouse franchises with massive payrolls knocked out embarrassingly by, again, these sort of plucky, well-managed, smart, strategic teams. And what was fun about this World Series, we didn't get the seven-game trauma, which is always great. But you had in the Rays and in the Brewers, of course, the opportunity to see a team that had never won this win this. And that's what we saw on Wednesday night. Stephanie Sy: For all the celebrations, no doubt happening in Milwaukee right now, there's a storm brewing over the MLB, as you know. The players and owners are headed toward a potential lockout with owners wanting these player salary caps. How does this World Series outcome weigh in on either side of this debate over salary caps? Jason Gay: Well, in a funny way, it's kind of a nightmare for baseball ownership, which very much wants a salary cap. They want the ceiling, they want a floor, maybe, but they definitely want a ceiling in the same way you have in basketball, football, other sports. When a team like the Rays comes forward, when a team like the Brewers comes forward and does it on a shoestring budget, it gives ammunition to the players to say, hey, look we don't need a cap. You guys just need to be better managed. You just have to be smarter with your money. What do we need a cap for? I still think that the ownership is going to be very, very adamant about getting that cap. And we could see a lockout situation, which really would be a terrible setup for the league. Stephanie Sy: Well, I know this is a story you're going to be following in coming weeks. Jason Gay with The Wall Street Journal, thank you. Jason Gay: Thank you.

e6cbde931621.text: By — Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Mary Clare Jalonick, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/senate-is-skeptical-about-making-daylight-saving-time-permanent-despite-trumps-pressure Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Senate is skeptical about making daylight saving time permanent despite Trump's pressure Politics Oct 29, 2026 6:19 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate is unlikely to act before the end of the year on a House-passed bill that would make daylight saving time permanent, defying President Donald Trump and dashing the hopes of Americans who don't like having to change their clocks twice a year. As daylight saving time ends early Sunday and much of the country turns the clocks back an hour, several senators are holding up legislation that would eliminate the longtime U.S. practice. Supporters argue that ending the time change would provide more daylight during the afternoon, when Americans are most active, but opponents say commuters in some states wouldn't see the sun until after 9 a.m. READ MORE: Daylight saving time is coming to an end again. Here's how the time change may impact you "No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter," said Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Cotton, a member of GOP leadership, is the most vocal opponent of the change, notably drawing Trump's ire earlier this month when the Republican president posted his personal cellphone number on social media and ordered him to "GET IT DONE!" But Cotton is not the only senator blocking the legislation, which would make daylight saving time the permanent national standard. READ MORE: America already tried permanent daylight saving time. Could it work now? Several other Republicans, particularly those from some Northern states that would see much later sunrises, say they also oppose it. "You'd be sending kids to school in the dark," said South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. Trump's pressure campaign hasn't worked Trump has aggressively pushed the change, putting pressure on Senate Republicans to pass the House bill and send it to his desk. In the posts targeting Cotton earlier this month, Trump wrote that sunshine is better in the afternoon than the morning and "CRIMINALS DON'T LIKE WORKING IN THE LIGHT." He renewed his call in a social media post this week, writing on Truth Social that "United States Senate is letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it." An avid golfer, Trump has made clear that adding daylight hours would mean more time to hit the links. He has argued that changing the time can be dangerous, especially when "you have high and dangerous steeples to reach, like on churches and municipal buildings." WATCH: Ditch the switch? Senators debate future of daylight saving time Even as many Americans now rely on digital clocks that change on their own, Trump said that "nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year." The president's arguments don't appear to have changed many votes in the Senate, however. Cotton has doubled down in response to Trump's pressure, and several Republicans predicted in recent weeks that the bill won't come up for a vote in the short time left when the Senate returns to Washington after the Nov. 3 midterm election. Sen. Todd Young, R-Ind., said that it's his understanding that the House bill is a "non-starter" for Senate Republican leaders. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio was even more blunt when asked this month if he thinks the bill will pass the Senate anytime soon. "No way," Moreno said. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., hasn't weighed in publicly on the House bill, but he has voted against similar versions in the past. Previous laws have been repealed In the winter of 1973, amid an energy crisis, Congress passed a law instituting permanent daylight saving time for what was supposed to be a trial period. But it was repealed by that October as public support had sharply dropped, partly because of concern for children who were walking to school in the dark. Now more than 50 years later, fewer Americans recall that experiment. Like Trump, many want to ditch the twice-yearly time change and add more daylight hours later in the day. An AP-NORC poll last year found that only 12% of American adults were in favor of the current system, while almost half opposed it. Proponents of a single time include the American Medical Association and American Academy of Sleep Medicine. Florida Sen. Rick Scott signed legislation when he was governor in 2018 that would allow the state to remain on daylight saving time year round, pending federal approval. Now in the Senate, the Republican has led efforts to make that happen. "I hear from Americans constantly that they are sick and tired of changing their clocks twice a year — it's an unnecessary, decades-old practice that's more of an annoyance to families than benefit to them," Scott said. Several Democrats are on board, as well. "The head-spinning ritual of falling back and springing forward has a very real impact on our economy, our health, and our happiness," said Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, when Scott introduced his own bill last year. "Let's say goodbye to 4pm winter sunsets." Associated Press writer Darlene Superville contributed to this report. Google parent Alphabet lost just over $500bn (Â£374bn) in value on Thursday after it rattled Wall Street with its last update of the year on its business operations.
Google spooked investors so badly that its stock hit a six-month low, after it revealed its artificial intelligence (AI) summaries on search were affecting ad revenue.
Microsoft and Amazon also updated investors this week, and joined Google in plans to keep spending astronomical sums of cash in an ongoing AI race.
But investors appeared dismayed at the impacts these plans are having on the ability of each to keep growing their core lines of business.
Google AI is eating its core business - search
At first glance, the quarterly results of Alphabet, the parent company of Google, were not at all bad.
Total revenue grew 25% compared to last year, hitting $127.6bn. It was buoyed by the ongoing success of Google Cloud, where revenue grew by 103% to almost $31bn.
However, profits at the company fell by a considerable 25% during the quarter. And for the second time in its history as a public company, it showed negative free cash flow, this time in excess of $9bn. That's almost twice the loss of cash Alphabet showed just three months ago.
Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Alphabet is now spending more money than it is bringing in. That new level of spending is almost entirely dedicated to Google's AI investments.
By the end of Thursday, the company's total stock market value had fallen to $3.46 trillion from $3.97 trillion the day before.
Google's omnipresent search engine now defaults to AI summaries of a person's query, and that hit the number of advertisements it was able to sell during the quarter.
The sale of ads that appear alongside Google Search results is the vast majority of Alphabet's business.
Tracy Woo, a principal analyst at Forrester, said Alphabet's disappointing search business results "highlights the challenge of funding massive AI investments while maintaining the strength of established businesses."
Although Phillip Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said on Wednesday that he felt "very good about our trajectory" with an AI-focused version of the search engine, the company's stock fell by almost 13% on Thursday, its second lowest showing this year.
Investors not buying Amazon's trillion-dollar business hopes
Amazon's stock also took a hit on Thursday after it shared results that disappointed investors. Shares of the company fell 6% in after hours stock trading.
Alongside quarterly sales growth of 11%, hitting $201bn, the company shared a staggering cash flow figure of negative $42bn.
That number shows that Amazon is not only spending more money than it makes, but that spending has increased six-fold over the span of three months.
Chief executive Andy Jassy claimed the business was spending in part because it had the chance at, not one, but two businesses that could end up bringing in $1 trillion for Amazon the future.
Jassy did not specify what two Amazon businesses those may be. But during a call with financial analysts he repeatedly mentioned the financial opportunity presented by Amazon making and selling its own computer chips, as well as its AI developer platform Bedrock, which offers paying users access to most major AI models and tools.
"One of the lessons we've learned over 20-plus years is that there is not one tool to rule the world," Jassy said. "People always assume whatever is in the lead early on will be the only thing that people use - it's never true."
As Jassy was asked several times to explain the company's spending, he admitted it "would be more convenient" if it were spread over the next 25 years. "That's not the world we live in," he added.
"We can fund this plan, and I think it will forever change the size, the revenue, the free cash flow of Amazon."
Microsoft begs the question of AI's real value
Wall Street reacted less enthusiastically to Microsoft's update, with shares falling by less than 1% on Thursday.
The company, which is also one of OpenAI's largest investors, spent around $5bn less on investments dedicated to AI. It also revealed earlier this week plans to cut thousands of workers, which will further reduce the company's costs.
Meanwhile, its revenue grew 19% from a year earlier, hitting $92.3bn for the quarter. Its crucial cloud business grew by 30% to $63bn.
Chief executive Satya Nadella said the use of Copilot, Microsoft's AI chatbot and tool, has seen "automated tasks nearly double since July" as daily users grew by 500% from a year ago.
Usually lower spending and growing sales earns a positive reaction from investors.
But Woo said Wall Street is trying to look farther into the future when it comes to which businesses will truly make good on their big promises around AI.
"Microsoft's results reinforce that enterprise demand for AI remains strong, but they also highlight a much bigger question facing the technology industry, where AI value will ultimately be captured," Woo said.

bf484f4d8dcd.text: The Pentagon's top military planner admitted to leaking classified information about Ukraine and Iran to two reporters from separate outlets over a one-year period, according to an internal report of the investigation shared with Axios. Why it matters: Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was fired this week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for the alleged misconduct, which the career soldier acknowledged on video after he failed four polygraph tests, a U.S. official said. "He had trouble passing multiple polygraph interviews," the report said. The report accused the general of making "unauthorized disclosures to the media," and said he "was cooperative with answering questions about interactions with the media to resolve this, and provided his personal phone for a forensics examination." Zoom in: The report and U.S. officials said that Sylvia's leaking began as early as June 2025 — before mainstream media outlets were removed from the Pentagon — and continued afterward via secure Signal app and once at a Silver Diner in Arlington, Va. "The meeting at the diner occurred because [redacted's] access to the Pentagon was revoked between meetings," the report says. "During the meeting at the diner, [Sylvia] relied on notes he took while reviewing a classified secret report to orally give redacted on U.S. assistance to Ukraine, the report says. The report says the reporter in question was writing a book and met twice with Sylvia. It also emphasized that the general "did not coordinate these meetings with [the Pentagon's Public Affairs Office], or seek to have the information reviewed before providing it to the reporter." The intrigue: U.S. officials suspect that Sylvia intentionally deleted any trace of contact on Signal between him and one of the reporters, but pretended it was an accident. "Sometime between June or July, Sylvia received Signal messages from [redacted]. Sylvia is unable to recall exactly what was in that message," the report said. "But he believes it had something to do with Iran." "He stated that he did not respond to the message and instead deleted it. While deleting it, he believes he deleted the entire message thread with [redacted]," the report said. "This erased Signal messages and Signal phone calls that would have been recorded in Signal on his personal phone." For another story, the report said, Sylvia "admitted to being one of the 20 officials" cited in a story criticizing Pentagon leadership. Another U.S. official told Axios that Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and his office lobbied the Joint Staff to put out a statement supporting Sylvia "to minimize the damage about any future claims of him leaking classified information." After someone within the Defense Department revealed to the Joint Staff why Sylvia was fired, the Joint Staff retracted its statement. Sylvia's dismissal marks the latest crackdown on leakers and the press from Hegseth's Pentagon. In July, the Defense Department announced a joint task force with the Justice Department that aimed to identify Pentagon leakers. It also called on the Pentagon's Office of General Counsel to prioritize prosecutions of those who make unauthorized disclosures to the media. Last year, in response to restrictive rules imposed by the Pentagon, several defense reporters and media outlets turned in their media passes. What they're saying: Sylvia did not immediately respond to a phone call, voicemail and text message left at the phone number listed for him in public records.

eb69976f8f92.text: By — Liz Landers Liz Landers By — Dan Cooney Dan Cooney By — Joshua Barajas Joshua Barajas By — Steff Staples Steff Staples By — Kelsey Paul Kelsey Paul Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/5-expert-takeaways-on-2026-midterm-election-security Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 5 expert takeaways on 2026 midterm election security Politics Oct 29, 2026 5:35 PM EDT With Election Day around the corner, states have been working hard to prepare, with some adopting new congressional maps and voting rules on top of normal election security measures. While President Donald Trump persists in making unfounded claims about the security and integrity of the nation's elections, the Department of Justice is planning to send 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states, more than double the number dispatched during the 2022 midterms. READ MORE: How some states are responding to DOJ's plan to send 1,000 monitors on Election Day As part of our coverage of the midterm groundwork happening across the country, PBS News' Liz Landers and Votebeat editorial director Jessica Huseman hosted a Reddit "Ask Me Anything" Q&A on Wednesday to address people's questions on election security. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Several questions touched on people's concerns about their vote being tampered with or not being counted, alongside broader concerns about possible meddling from the federal government. The Trump administration is attempting measures that haven't been tried before, Huseman said. Those actions include attempts to change election rules through executive orders, repeated demands for voter data and efforts to expand the government's role – specifically the executive branch – in elections. All of this amounts to an "unprecedented environment now," she said. And yet, "elections officials are confident the system will hold," she added. Here are five major takeaways from the Reddit AMA. Evidence shows that illegal voting is extremely rare Ballots for the upcoming midterm elections are stacked inside a locked, secured and monitored cage at the Durham County Board of Elections, as election officials boost security to fortify the building and protect staff in preparation for the upcoming midterm elections, in Durham, North Carolina, on Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Jonathan Drake/ Reuters Trump has routinely cast doubt on the security of the vote, making false claims of "rampant" voter fraud even a week ahead of Nov. 3. The president, who has continued to falsely claim that the 2020 presidential election was "rigged," has fixated on rooting out what he claims is election fraud this election cycle. The Trump administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas to more than a dozen states requesting voter roll data, expanding its efforts to tamp down alleged noncitizen voting. But illegal voting by noncitizens voting is vanishingly rare. READ MORE: Trump's focus on noncitizen voting has led to 160 arrests. That shows it's rare, experts say Votebeat spent more than a year investigating claims from a group called the Election Truth Alliance that promoted a statistical analysis suggesting votes in the 2024 election had been manipulated in Pennsylvania, she said. The nonprofit newsroom consulted nearly a dozen experts and put the Election Truth Alliance's claims through peer review. "What we actually found was that the model would identify fraud even on datasets intentionally built not to contain any fraud," Huseman said. "Despite much of their analysis not standing up to scrutiny, it still managed to raise more than $400,000 in a single year." WATCH: Inside Georgia's push to rebuild trust in elections after Trump's false claims Huseman said it's worth remembering that "elections are not black boxes." "In the places where the Election Truth Alliance alleged truly incredible problems, there were audits, observers, paper ballots and an entire staff of people whose jobs are ensuring the accuracy of these numbers," she said. "We can scrutinize the evidence as it's presented, but when we have it, we have to look it squarely in the face and call it what it is." Trump can't declare a national emergency to interfere with elections Nowhere in the U.S. Constitution does the president of the United States have express authority over how elections are run. As laid out in the country's founding document, states determine the time, place and manner of elections. And Congress has a role in passing legislation over federal elections, though they have not passed major laws like this in a while, Landers said. READ MORE: Immigrants seeking U.S. citizenship targeted in Trump administration's illegal voting crackdown To put a finer point on it: The president cannot declare some kind of national emergency and expect all 50 states to stop their elections. "I know from speaking with election officials across the country that they will not stop their election administration just because the president declared something over a process he does not have any legal authority," Landers said. She also asked Trump in February if he would declare a national emergency — as some of his allies have urged. He said no at the time, adding he'd never heard about that. Federal election monitors are there to observe The Justice Department is planning to dispatch more than 1,000 federal election monitors to observe proceedings on Election Day. What they can do at polling places is fairly limited. WATCH: DOJ monitoring plans and DHS voter checks raise concerns of election interference To be clear: Federal election monitors are a normal part of both midterm and presidential elections, and the Biden administration deployed them in the 2024 presidential election cycle. Six military freezers went bad in August. Was it a cyber attack?
After food spoiled at commissaries, Pentagon investigators are looking at similar incidents in France.
The Pentagon is investigating a suspected cyberattack behind freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the United States in August, according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter.
The outages affected some six commissaries — the on-base grocery stores serving military personnel — per the official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the situation. At Fort Huachuca in Arizona, officials reported that a freezer had entered defrost mode and heated its contents, leaving food spoiled.
Reuters first reported Thursday that investigators were treating the incidents as a possible hack. It’s unclear who might be responsible or whether investigators have conclusively determined what caused the failures.
Cyber Command and various Defense Department law-enforcement units are probing the incident. French authorities are also working with officials examining the matter. Earlier this month, hackers overrode temperature controls on commercial refrigeration equipment at more than 350 French establishments, forcing supermarkets to discard spoiled food.
The investigation draws attention to the computers that control everyday equipment used to store and handle food, an often overlooked area of cybersecurity where a hack can spoil supplies or interrupt distribution of goods.
The unusual U.S. outages and the possibility of hacking were initially flagged in August by the Signal and Silence blog. Stars and Stripes subsequently reported the involvement of military investigators, and The Telegraph also reported officials’ contact with French authorities.
A 2021 DHS assessment of threats to food and agriculture specifically identified refrigeration failures and shipping delays as cybersecurity risks that could cause spoilage and shortages.
The Food and Agriculture Information Sharing and Analysis Center, an industry group that shares cyber threat intelligence on the nation's food supply, has warned that attackers are targeting internet-accessible industrial controls that may not have optimal cyberdefenses in place.
The agri-food sector’s sensitivity to downtime often gives ransomware groups leverage to demand payment, the organization said in a separate report.
Lawmakers have sought to improve federal protections. A bipartisan group reintroduced the Farm and Food Cybersecurity Act in 2025, following an earlier proposal introduced in 2024.

The main Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and Arab-led party leaders have denounced Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleging foreign interference following the election which saw his coalition lose its majority.
Netanyahu's Likud accused Israel's Arab-led parties of "stealing" the election. Home security agency Shin Bet is investigating whether they received illegal funding from Qatar and Turkey.
Qatar's foreign ministry denied the "ridiculous and dangerous" allegations and accused Israeli politicians of conducting a disinformation campaign against Doha.
Final results confirmed that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the Jewish opposition had won a majority in parliament.
The two Arab party lists - The Joint List and the Ra'am - defied expectations to win a record 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers, with Netanyahu's bloc winning 53 seats and his rival Gadi Eisenkot's bloc securing 48.
On Thursday Likud alleged that voters had been "bribed" to vote for Arab parties, after the head of the Central Elections Committee (CEC) asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate "serious suspicions" of foreign interference.
Both Arab parties strongly rejected the claim, with the Arab-majority Joint List alliance saying it was baseless.
The row is being seen by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to delegitimise the Arab parties, thereby making it politically impossible for Eisenkot to join forces with them - which is currently his bloc's only route to power.
Israeli media reported that the CEC had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's Foreign Ministry "categorically" denied the claims.
Netanyahu and his Likud Party framed the allegations as a "political earthquake" and an "an attack on democracy", aimed at removing their right-wing government.
But the Shin Bet later clarified that their investigation did not implicate an entire community who had voted legally, while acting CEC Director General Dean Livne said there was "no basis for allegations of systematic violations of election integrity."
Eisenkot, who was briefed on the investigation, said "it is too early to determine what happened, or if anything happened at all," and accused Netanyahu of running "an orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results".
Balad chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, who is part of the Joint List, dismissed the allegation, saying: "The losing side is constructing a racist blood libel and calling on the security agencies to use force in order to overturn the election results."
Netanyahu's attacks on Arab voters and parties have been ongoing for days. He spent much of election day posting on social media that high Arab turnout is an "emergency" and a "matter of life or death" for the Israeli right. He also shared AI-generated images of Arab voters at polling stations, in an attempt to encourage right-wingers to get out and vote.
Arab Israelis, many of whom refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel, make up about one fifth of the country.
For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout on Tuesday was inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, led by Netanyahu.
The final results offer only three plausible options for a government to be formed: a national unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but speculation has swirled in recent days that an agreement could yet be reached.
A snap poll conducted by Hebrew University showed that the most popular option for voters from every party in the opposition bloc was for Eisenkot to form a minority government with Ra'am, and supported from outside by the Joint List.

f0d8e1dc1d05.text: Reddit on Thursday said it's moving to become a primarily logged-in experience, marking one of the most significant shifts in its 21-year history. Why it matters: Reddit has long championed the open web. Now, it's pushing to build a more direct relationship with users while also protecting its data from increased scraping in the AI era. Driving the news: In an interview Thursday, Reddit co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman said the company is making the change to improve its user experience, bolster its ads business and prevent bots from scraping its proprietary data. Chief operating officer Jen Wong told Axios the move doesn't represent a change in strategy as the company has always focused on building a direct destination. "It's just that in the last 10 years, because our [data] corpus was open, we got a lot of search traffic, so that became part of the equation" but didn't change the company's mission. Zoom in: Huffman expressed confidence that the change would ultimately improve engagement and monetization, even as changes to traditional search continue to impact user growth in the U.S. "When users log in, they spend more time on Reddit, and we can we better know their interests, so we can target ads better," he said. He also noted that the short-term risk is limited because "the vast majority of engagement and over 80% of our monetization comes from our app and logged-in users." In a shareholder letter, Reddit acknowledged that search referral traffic was "down meaningfully in Q3" and said daily users could decline by a "low-double-digit percentage" in Q4 if search referral trends persist. How it works: Reddit will begin testing the fully logged-in experience this quarter outside the U.S. and collect data on the best approach before it rolls out broader changes gradually. Logged-in users can get tailored content, feeds and recommended communities based on their activity and interests, although they can opt out of personalization. The company is still working through what content will be available to users who do not login. Participation features, such as commenting and content ranking, will continue to be accessible only to logged-in users. Its homepage will still be accessible to logged-out visitors. People accessing the platform via search engines or shared links will still be able to see that linked content. Huffman said the company will monitor the conversion rate to logged-in users as one metric of success. Between the lines: Reddit has long prioritized user privacy and has supported user anonymity as a way to encourage authentic expression. Logged-in users will not be required to reveal their real name or real-world identity, the company said. The company is relaunching its incognito browsing mode within its app, which lets users browse and search without affecting their logged-in accounts. But the platform will be read-only in incognito mode, meaning users can't comment or engage. Follow the money: The changes will make user personalization more central to the Reddit experience, which Wong said will bolster the company's ads business. Logged-in user engagement is about five times that of logged-out users, Wong said. "They see more impressions, and therefore, yield more business outcomes for advertisers," she noted. Performance advertising, which now amounts to more than 60% of Reddit's ad revenue, is the fastest-growing part of the company's business. Reality check: Most other major consumer internet platforms have already made this shift. Huffman said he personally resisted the changes because of his belief in the open internet. He ultimately came around because Reddit's scale made personalization more important for users today and because protecting the platform's content from unauthorized scraping has become more urgent. The company said most of its unauthorized scrapes are of content that lives outside of the logged-in experience on the open web. The big picture: The change was announced alongside Reddit's Q3 earnings results, which saw the ads business grow a whopping 54% year over year. The company beat Wall Street estimates on revenue and earnings growth, but missed expectations on U.S. user growth amid weakened search traffic. Since going public in March 2024, Reddit's ads business has nearly tripled. The company earned $222.7 million in ad revenue in Q1 2024, compared with $847 million in Q3 this year. The vast majority of Reddit's revenue (94.7%) comes from ads. Zoom out: Reddit believes its content will become more valuable in the AI era, as people look for authentic human recommendations and content to validate information from chatbots. "We are a collection of human experiences and preferences that is extremely vast and fresh, and I don't think there's anything comparable to it," Wong said. As of Q3, Reddit has more than 27 billion posts and comments, an unprecedented trove of human data. Reddit will still license its content to third parties and rely on those agreements to set equitable terms for scraping and content usage. In its earnings release, the company said revenue outside of advertising, which includes data licensing, totaled $48 million in third quarter, up 35% year over year. What to watch: The shift to logged-in users will help Reddit be more intentional about third-party access to its data. Huffman explained the way that data is used and displayed on other platforms can impact the core experience of Reddit. Reddit announced an expanded partnership with Google in 2024, reportedly with $60 million annually. It announced a similar deal with OpenAI later that year. The company sued Anthropic and Perplexity in 2025 for unauthorized scraping. The bottom line: Huffman said the shift is not a response to Google Search changes, but rather "about making the best version of Reddit." In five years, "I want Reddit to be more Reddit," he remarked, saying he hopes the changes help users lean into the platform's core experiences, like intentional communities and up-or-

051d757f798c.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/judge-blocks-trump-administrations-medicaid-work-requirement-rule-forcing-proof-of-medical-frailty Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge blocks Trump administration's Medicaid work requirement rule forcing proof of medical frailty Health Oct 29, 2026 3:53 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Chronically ill people on Medicaid won't be bound by new work requirement rules that the latest Trump administration guidance requires in order to qualify for "medically frail" exemptions, a federal judge ruled Thursday. U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston gave a partial victory to a coalition of 25 states and the District of Columbia, which sued the Trump administration in June over the new Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services guidance linked to the 2025 law known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill." READ MORE: As states face stricter Medicaid work requirements, Nebraska is an early test The law says the definition of medically frail must include people who are blind or disabled, have substance use disorders or disabling mental disorders, have certain disabilities that significantly impair daily activities, or have serious or complex medical conditions. But the CMS rule went further, requiring people in those categories to show that their conditions also "significantly impair" their ability to comply with the law's work requirements. The plaintiffs argued that the stricter rule would prevent eligible Americans from accessing the care they need — and oversteps the text of the law itself as well. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "The states have met their burden of showing irreparable harm for which monetary damages would provide inadequate compensation — they face the burden of costly and intensive alterations to their eligibility verification systems," Stearns said in his 16-page ruling. Notably, while the ruling will make it easier for some Medicaid recipients with qualifying medical conditions to obtain an exemption from the new work requirements, Stearns' decision does not strike down the work requirements as unlawful. Additionally, Stearns upheld two other federal restrictions on how states can verify medical frailty: including the requirement that states reject proof of patients' medical frailty if the diagnosis is more than a year old. He also upheld a policy allowing states to accept only one self-attestation per continuous period of enrollment. Explaining why he upheld the portions in favor of the government, Stearns said "the government provided a non-frivolous rationale for adopting each provision and explained why it did not find the States' concerns of disenrollment compelling." Representatives from the Department of Health and Human Services and CMS did not immediately respond to an Associated Press request for comment. The new Medicaid restrictions are part of Trump's big tax and policy law in 2025. The change affects those covered through an expansion in most states that gave more lower-income people access to the government's safety net healthcare program. Starting Jan. 1, expansion enrollees aged 19 to 64 must show that they work or do community service at least 80 hours a month, or are in school at least half the time. There are exceptions for those considered medically frail or in addiction treatment programs, among others. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Thick fog has formed on Friday morning across parts of the United Kingdom which could lead to hazardous driving conditions.
The Met Office has issued a yellow severe weather warning for fog from Lincolnshire, the East Midlands, the Home Counties into parts of Greater London.
Fog will be dense in places with visibility below 100 metres at times and it will be most extensive and disruptive during the morning rush hour.
It will slowly begin to thin, lift and clear later this morning but in some rural spots in eastern England it may not clear until this afternoon.
The weekend forecast
Early morning mist and fog patches on Saturday may lift into low cloud, which could hang around all day.
Some areas will fare better with some spells of sunshine with many areas staying dry.
The exception to this theme will be north-west Scotland, where a weak weather front will bring thicker cloud and rain for a time.
Temperatures will be close to average and will be overall, similar to recent days.
By Sunday this dying weather front will bring some thicker cloud to Wales and central England threatening a few patches of light rain or drizzle, but not much.
The rest of the UK will have a dry day on Sunday with variable cloud and some spells of sunshine at times.
When will we see Storm Chloe?
High pressure has been building and is set to dominate across the UK in the coming days.
This is in stark contrast to last week which saw areas buffeted by a cluster of storms developed by a powerful Atlantic jet stream.
The jet stream, still running close to the UK, with the building area of high pressure bringing us much quieter weather.
Whilst Storms Austen and Boelo provided some short-term hydrological benefit, 82% of England remains in drought status according to the Environment Agency.
The area of high pressure will stay over or close to the UK for at least ten days as a result of a 'diffluent blocking pattern' forming in the Atlantic jet stream across the UK and western Europe, which will prevent weather systems reaching our shores.
It means we are heading into a long stretch of mostly dry weather. There could still be some patches of low cloud and drizzle associated with early morning mist and fog, however, rainfall amounts will be negligible.
With no storms on the horizon any time soon, it is likely to be a while before we see the arrival of Chloe, the next name on this year's storm list.
In the short-term this lack of rainfall will raise concerns about the drought and low water levels in England's reservoirs.
Following the latest meeting of the National Drought Group, water companies are being urged to speed up the fixing of leaks and members of the public to take shorter showers and turn off the tap when brushing their teeth.
The Environment Agency (EA) says that 20% more rain than average is needed over the next six months, external for the drought to end.
Philip Duffy, Chief Executive of the Environment Agency, said: "The recent rain is welcome, but the drought isn't over. A few wet days cannot reverse months of hot, dry weather.
"Our rivers, reservoirs and groundwater need sustained rainfall to recover, and the effects on nature can last much longer."
El NiÃ±o has been linked to wetter and stormier weather in late autumn and early winter. The current three month outlook from the Met Office forecasts that there is double the chance of it being wetter than normal.

Conservationists have completed the purchase of a huge upland estate following a two-year Â£30m public appeal backed by the likes of Sir David Attenborough.
The Wildlife Trusts - a federation of 47 conservation charities - and Northumberland Wildlife Trust (NWT) plan to "enhance the rich natural heritage" of the Rothbury Estate, a 9,500-acre stretch of former grouse moor, woodland and farmland - having headed off fears it could be split among multiple owners.
Broadcaster Sir David described it as an opportunity "to create something very special for generations to come".
Not everyone supported the campaign, though, with some local farmers having warned the purchase would be "a folly".
Owned by Lord Max Percy, the Duke of Northumberland's youngest son, the estate had been in the family for about 700 years and was understood to be the largest area of land put up for sale in England in decades.
Worried public access could become more difficult if it was divided between owners, the wildlife organisations bought an initial tract in 2024 covering the Simonside Hills and a mixture of lowland, woods, riverside and farmland.
That also saw them strike a deal to purchase the remainder of the estate if they could raise the Â£30m in two years with ambitions for it to become a 40-mile (64km) "wild" corridor, stretching from the North East coast to Kielder and the Scottish border.
It has now been announced they have taken out a "low-interest loan to bridge the short-term funding gap between pledged monies still to be received and the fundraising target, ensuring completion of the entire estate".
'Extraordinary landscape'
NWT chief executive Mike Pratt said the campaign had been "remarkable".
"Opportunities of this scale and significance are incredibly rare.
"By securing this extraordinary landscape, we've the potential to create a flagship for nature recovery supported by sustainable farming whilst delivering lasting benefits for wildlife, local people and the rural economy."
Backing last year by Sir David, who serves as president emeritus of the Wildlife Trusts, led to a surge in donations with more than Â£1m being brought in from across the globe in a week.
Commenting on the appeal's success, he said: "Now the opportunity to bring the vision of a landscape where nature and people thrive side by side can become a reality.
"This will be a place where nature, community, farming and heritage can combine to create something very special."
More than 25,000 people donated, NWT said, with other major contributions including a Â£5m grant from the National Lottery Heritage Fund in March this year.
This week it was announced the government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) had pledged Â£1.94m, taking the appeal to within touching distance of its target.
Why is the area so coveted?
The estate has a number of important wildlife habitats, conservationists say, with some already designated as Sites of Special Scientific Interest.
Species such as curlew, mountain bumblebee, lapwing and other wading birds have made it their home with endangered red squirrels finding safety in the woods.
Harebell, wild thyme and mountain pansy flower colourfully in summer months, with salmon and under-threat eels spotted in the rivers.
The wildlife trusts believe "this rich tapestry of wildlife could be richer still" if more species return over the next 10 years.
There are also hopes pine marten, beavers and ancient breeds of cattle could become common sights.
Opinion 'finely split'
The plan was not universally popular though.
Chris Armstrong, a tenant farmer overseeing 1,000 acres close to the site, was among those questioning it.
He told the BBC earlier this year the community was split over the issue: "The most recent strapline seems to be 'time is running out to save the Rothbury Estate'.
"The Rothbury Estate doesn't need saving. Saving from what?"
"I would put it very much akin to the Brexit vote, I would think it would be that finely split.
"I think the majority of the farming community see this as a folly."
Meanwhile, Defra's contribution has come under fire from Councillor Guy Renner-Thompson, chairman of Northumberland Conservatives.
He said the pledge showed the government "has its priorities wrong" in light of difficulties people across the country have faced securing sustainable farming incentive (SFI) funding.
"Farmers were left scrambling in an application window that opened and closed the same day," Renner-Thompson said.
"Yet ministers can find nearly Â£2m to help a charity buy an estate."
In response, Nature Minister Jenny Riddell-Carpenter said the government was "stepping in to help" having seen thousands of members of the public give their support for a "once-in-a-generation opportunity".

An Australian athlete has admitted putting others at risk by continuing to race after soiling herself during an endurance sports event.
Speaking exclusively to the BBC ahead of her return to the sport, Joanna Wietrzyk suggested her determination to win the Hyrox race in Beijing in September had clouded her judgement: "It was my decision to continue racing so I take full responsibility for that."
Challenged over why she carried on, she said: "I didn't really think about those around meâ¦ the decision that I made in hindsight was the wrong decision and I'm truly sorry for everyone that I did affect."
The 24-year-old said that the experience and subsequent backlash was "traumatic". She also said she had considered walking away from the sport, in which she holds a world record.
Hyrox sees participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises, including a sled push, burpee jumps, indoor rowing, and lunges while carrying a sandbag.
The competition has exploded in popularity since it was founded in 2017 in Hamburg, in northern Germany, and is now held across the world.
Roughly halfway through her event last month, Wietrzyk suffered a bout of diarrhoea. Images of faecal matter on parts of her body were then shared widely online.
Asked whether officials should have stopped her, she said no-one encouraged her to do so at the time.
Hyrox's co-founder, Moritz FÃ¼rste, has issued an apology saying it had been a mistake not to react immediately during the race.
New rules have now been introduced giving race directors the power to remove athletes if their vomit, urine or faeces pose a risk of contamination or threaten the welfare of themselves or others in a race that is primarily held indoors using shared equipment.
Although initially defiant in a now-deleted Instagram post, Wietrzyk apologised in the week after the Beijing event and said she would forfeit the win and retroactively withdraw from the race.
Due to compete in Hamburg on Friday, she said she was "nervous" about her return and hoped that the high-profile incident would not define her.
"I don't want it to become my identity," she said.
In her first interview since Beijing, Wietrzyk said she had suffered a bacterial infection from food poisoning but had gone into the race "feeling fresh, feeling really, really good".
"It was a very sudden experience," she told the BBC.
"It wasn't until about halfway through the race where everything did transpire... In that moment, right then and there, as a very competitive personâ¦ and an elite athlete that I am, my only focus is on racing.
"Obviously I did put other people at risk," she admitted.
Hyrox China has since reportedly refunded some competitors their entry fees.
Wietrzyk also said she regretted an initial social media post published after the race which included the words "Go hard or go home" and "a win is a win". She said she had been in "flight or fight mode" as she sought hospital treatment.
"I didn't really account for what the public would have seen that situation as."
Challenged over whether her apology could be seen as an effort at damage limitation, or too late, she said that she hadn't expected so much exposure from the incident.
"I needed those days to reflect on it and process it."
Speaking about the mentality of elite athletes, she said: "They're so hyper-vigilant on winning and doing the best that they can, putting their training to good use and showcasing their fitness to the world."
After reflecting over the past weeks, she said: "There is more to lifeâ¦ than just racing and just winning."
After Wietrzyk's identity was shared online, Hyrox said anyone sending abuse or threats to the athlete would be banned from future events.
Speaking about the comments and photo shares online Joanna Wietrzyk said there had both been support, to make sure she was OK, but that it had also shown social media can be a very "toxic place".
Wietrzyk told the BBC that it had been a "mentally and emotionally taxing period" and she had not expected the global scrutiny, saying her family had also received threats.
"[It] was very eye-opening for me to see the effect of social media nowadays, especially from someone who's 24, just out there racing.
"Yes, I did make the wrong decision but I don't believe I should have received such backlash and such scrutiny onlineâ¦ At the end of the day I'm only human."
Wietrzyk said had been trying to stay offline and had sought to "isolate herself from the world" for a time: "I can't do that forever."
"I still have so much more I can achieve in this sport so I think, for me, my mental resilience is the key here where I can inspire others through what I've been through."

Britain's largest ever woodland survey of bats would "simply not have been feasible" without AI, scientists say.
Researchers left devices on poles among the trees of 310 woodlands across Britain, recording 98 million bat calls over three years, which would have taken more than 30 years to analyse without AI.
Some of Britain's rarest and most threatened bats, including the red-listed Barbastelle, have been recorded in the south-west of England, including Somerset, Devon, Cornwall and Dorset.
Kate Jones, from University College London, said: "AI has fundamentally changed the scale at which we can monitor wildlife." She added the survey was a "nice story of AI for good".
More from Somerset
Jones added: "Previously, analysing this volume of acoustic data would simply not have been feasible.
"These efficient open-source AI tools allow us to identify millions of bat calls across thousands of nights of recordings, identify patterns and flag species at a national scale."
The Barbastelle roams ancient forests but its elusive nature has made it challenging to track.
Hotspots of Barbastelle activity detected in the survey were concentrated across the South West.
Lia Gilmour, of the Bat Conservation Trust, which was involved in the survey alongside Forest Research, said the project was "unprecedented".
"We're getting some really good bat activity in the south-west area of Somerset," Gilmour said.
"Somerset is generally a really good stronghold for the bat species we have across the UK.
"It's been quite exciting some of the rarest species popping up in Somerset as part of the survey.
"In biodiversity monitoring, we view AI as a powerful tool," Gilmour added.
"We were looking at huge volumes of data and 90,000 hours of recording, there was no way we would be able to do this manually."

Last month, protests erupted in squares and streets across Syria. People burned tyres, blocked roads and chanted slogans, angry at the government's decision to raise fuel prices again. It was the largest show of discontent yet since President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power two years ago.
Speaking on a Syrian TV channel, a man said he still supported the authorities but that his situation had deteriorated to the point where he could no longer afford to buy bread. "Honestly," another said, "we have begun to fear what kind of new decision each morning will bring".
The increase was the latest in a series of measures people blame for a growing cost-of-living crisis. For many Syrians, life, financially, has worsened since rebels led by Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad, ending five decades of his family's brutal rule and more than 13 years of a devastating civil war.
Catapulted to the presidency, Sharaa has, since then, led Syria's transition and efforts to revive a broken economy after a long period of mismanagement, isolation and conflict.
There was never any doubt about how challenging this would be. But as they celebrated Assad's overthrow and their new freedoms, Syrians, perhaps unrealistically, hoped things would quickly improve. That, however, has not materialised, and the handling of the economy has frustrated many here.
From essential bills to basic items, the cost of virtually everything has gone up. And many saw a further and unexpected rise in fuel prices as a sign of a government out of touch with its country.
"We don't want roundabouts. Every day they build a new roundabout. People stood by you and are still with you," another protester said, addressing Sharaa, "but this will [make] things explode".
Days later, amid calls for further demonstrations, the increase was revoked.
In a suburb of Damascus, I joined Fatima Saleh Eid at an open-air market for her weekly shop. At 50, she works as a cleaner to help support her family.
"We've suffered a lot," she said. Her husband had recently been hired by a ceramic factory after a year unemployed. He is among the lucky ones, as many are struggling to find work. In some streets, men gather in the hope of meeting someone offering a day job; often, they wait in vain.
Since coming to power, the government has slashed long-held subsidies as part of an austerity drive. The price of bread, a Syrian staple, has increased tenfold. Fuel prices are now in line with the international average, which has put pressure on farmers and made transportation more expensive, while the cost of electricity has gone up several hundred per cent for some.
The authorities, in response, have adjusted public sector wages, including pensions; unsurprisingly, the effect of the additional pay for people has been lost as prices keep rising.
"We eat more sparingly now. We can't afford chicken anymore nor meat. We only eat vegetables but even [that is] expensive," Fatima said. "Inshallah [God willing] things will get cheaper."
As she spoke, around a dozen people, of all ages, gathered around us. Nobody disagreed. One elderly man also said he had stopped eating meat. Another, in his 20s, told me his family were no longer able to pay the medicine for his father, who had a heart condition. One young woman said she and her four children could only afford to have a proper meal every two days.
Marwan Bashour, a 68-year-old pensioner, said his monthly pay was around $90 (Â£70), which is the public sector minimum wage. "It's not enough at all," he said.
The United Nations Development Programme said 90% of Syrians were in poverty last year.
Marwan told me how he made ends meet.
"Sometimes I borrow money, sometimes I sell things from my house," he said, "like an old pot or plates that we never used, gifts that were given to us. I've even had to sell furniture".
There have been other pressures too. Like many Syrians, Marwan used to rely on help from aid agencies. But, for him, that has stopped, as organisations have been forced to cut back services because of funding cuts.
Syria has also not been immune to the impact of the US-Iran war. The government said the fuel increase that led to the protests was, in part, due to the pressure on energy markets because of the conflict.
I met another pensioner, Nabil al-Remhein, who is 63. None of his four adult children could find work. "We're now having only one meal a day. It's tragic," he said. His face looked tired. "It isn't only me. It's the entire population. We're all hungry... We're suffocating under rising costs."
Nabil took me to his house, in a poor area of narrow alleys and modest buildings. There, I met his wife. She was doing her chores in the dark.
"I'm afraid of the electricity bill," Nabil said. "We've cut back on lighting up the house and we [also] turn off the fridge for about five hours a day".
Still, their latest bill was about a third of the family's income. He has not paid it.
Dr Haid Haid, a Syrian columnist and consulting fellow at the London-based think tank Chatham House, said a "significant portion of the population" was worse off than before Assad's fall.
The economic crisis, he told me, was "one of the most dangerous issues" for the government, and that some of it was of its own making.
"Part of [the crisis] is related to the lack of [financial] resources and the legacy left by the former regime," he said.
"But it's also the direct impact of the new policies that are moving [Syria] towards a liberal and free-market sort of economy, which don't take into account the impact on people".
A spokesman for the Syrian economy and industry ministry told me no-one was available for an interview.
Sharaa has, of course, scored some important gains.
International sanctions imposed in the Assad-era have been lifted, and the US has removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
Security remains volatile and a source of concern, but the country feels more stable.
