KWIGILLINGOK, Alaska—Lucy Martin’s family was among the last to be evacuated from Kwigillingok, a Yup’ik village a quarter mile from the Bering Sea that was devastated by Typhoon Halong in October 2025.
A year later, Martin, the village’s tribal resilience coordinator, is still in Bethel, a regional hub about 70 miles to the northeast, and is unsure when she and the other villagers can return home.
About 30 people are back in Kwigillingok, despite the village being largely unlivable due to the damage to housing stock and critical infrastructure, such as boardwalks, plumbing and the community water pipeline. But most of the 361 residents who lived there before the storm are sheltered in Bethel, Anchorage and several nearby communities. The post-disaster recovery has been slow, and the village remains under a ‘no-go-home’ order.
“I have no house,” Martin said. “All of our tribal leaders have no homes to go to.”
In the wee hours of October 12, 2025, the remnants of Typhoon Halong, which had reached Category 4 strength near Japan, slammed into southwestern Alaska, impacting over 40 communities in the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta and destroying the Alaska Native Villages of Kwigillingok and Kipnuk. Southwestern winds and a high tide supercharged by the full moon drove a storm surge into Kwigillingok, reaching over 6.3 ft above the normal highest tide line—more than twice as high as the previous record.
The village became the sea. The surge lifted 46 of 99 houses off their foundations and carried them for miles, most with their inhabitants trapped inside. The water ripped boardwalks from the ground, downed power lines and washed away snowmobiles, ATVs and boats, as well as freezers packed with months of food. Caskets from the cemetery rolled in the waves. Three people died.
The evacuation of about 1,500 people from the villages of Kwigillingok, Kipnuk and Nightmute was the largest domestic rescue operation in Alaska history. The scale of damage is still being assessed, and, although it was recognized as a federal disaster, the recovery from Halong, delayed by multiple shutdowns of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, including the Federal Emergency Management Agency, will take years.
This year, Kwigillingok and Kipnuk voted to relocate to higher ground. But neither federal nor state disaster recovery funding is designed to help communities move out of harm’s way.
But the rebuilding of Kwigillingok has also stalled.
Alaska has short and expensive construction seasons, but despite the mild weather, Kwigillingok had no crews on the ground from early September to mid-October. The spokesperson for the Department of Transportation and Public Facilities, the state agency tasked with clearing the debris, restoring roadways and stabilizing structures, said that construction crews waited for FEMA funding to resume work.
Wreckage has been removed, but debris remains in the village. Some boardwalks elevated above the soggy tundra have been restored and reinforced, but many are still broken. About 13 houses have been partially repaired, Martin said. Others are in the tundra, sideways, or piled up against each other like dominoes. Homes are overrun with mold. The school, though largely undamaged, remains indefinitely closed. Two solemn rows of about 50 caskets are lined up on a boardwalk, waiting for a mass re-internment. Seven more are still in the tundra.
The villagers who have returned have little to survive on as Kwigillingok prepares for its second winter since the disaster.
The state of Alaska has already committed $75 million to recovery efforts, and that tally will keep growing as damages and needs increase. FEMA has approved and largely paid out $62.9 million in individual and housing assistance to more than 2,500 households, plus an additional $40.2 million in other assistance, including for subsistence equipment, such as fishing gear, fish racks and smokehouses. FEMA has also set aside almost $9 million for the State of Alaska to repair or replace critical infrastructure and facilities in all impacted communities. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the Small Business Administration and several dozen other federal, state, and Alaska Native agencies are also involved in the recovery.
But these amounts fall far short of what the region needs to recover from the unprecedented storm.
The state of Alaska asked FEMA for additional Permanent Housing Construction funding and was denied after eight months of waiting. This funding program, authorized in the Stafford Act for Insular States and Territories, may provide home repair and construction services where regular streams of FEMA funding are not feasible or cost-effective.
Bryan Fisher, the Director of the Alaska Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management, told Inside Climate News that the denial brought more delays on the ground. The state is preparing to appeal that decision, he said.
Fisher estimates the total cost of post-Halong recovery will surpass $400 million, requiring greater buy-in from the federal government.
Darell John, one of the few residents who stayed in the village after the evacuation, is frustrated with the speed and quality of the recovery, and the poor communication between the village and the agencies intended to help it.
According to John, the DOT’s crews didn’t consult the community or its leadership about which houses to repair and fixed several homes that were uninhabited before the storm. Some exterior sewage flush tanks—called “dog houses”—are improperly affixed to the houses and will not survive subarctic winters, he said.
John described the work as a “bad investment.” “They could have invested in getting portable homes that community members can come back to and stay [in] until the new site is ready,” he said.
Martin, the tribal resilience coordinator, agreed, adding that repairing drenched, mold-infested houses was ill-advised and “a big waste of money.”

If you’re an ordinary resident of Pennsylvania and you want to dispose of potentially toxic waste, the Department of Environmental Protection will direct you to specialized dropoff locations: recycling programs or local events where officials collect things like propane tanks and pharmaceuticals.
If you’re in the oil and gas business, your options may become much more expansive this year. The DEP quietly issued a new permit in May that experts warn will make it easier for the industry to dump toxic, radioactive waste directly onto roadways.
“It’s ridiculous on its face, in my view,” said David Hess, a former DEP secretary who maintains the PA Environment Digest blog, tracking environmental actions across the state.
The new permit means companies could reclassify conventional, or non-fracked, oil and gas wells as “mineral brine” wells, which would allow them to sell radioactive wastewater as a product. It can then be spread across roads to control dust and eliminate ice in the winter. Any oil or gas produced from those wells could also be sold as waste.
Pennsylvania produces more gas than any other state in the nation besides Texas, and alongside that gas comes millions of gallons of toxic wastewater. This waste, also known as brine because of its high salt content, contains heavy metals and radioactive elements such as radium. For decades, “roadspreading,” slathering oil and gas wastewater across roads to de-ice them and reduce dust, spread pollutants throughout the state.
Even setting aside environmental and health concerns and the bizarre regulatory framework that undergirds this dumping, when it comes to reducing dust, the brine “doesn’t do what it purports to do,” said Charlie Palladino, a policy advocate at the environmental nonprofit Earthworks. Siri Lawson, a resident of Farmington Township in Warren County who blames exposure to oil and gas waste for her ongoing respiratory problems, was more direct: “It seemed to make the dust worse,” she said.
Academic research backs this up, suggesting that the wastewater controls dust no better than rainwater. It can also inadvertently damage paved roads, “turning them into something that looks like Swiss cheese,” said Hess.
A study from Penn State found that roadspreading releases roughly four times more radium into the surrounding environment than wastewater facilities and 200 times more than isolated spills. The practice was common until 2018, when Lawson filed an appeal with the state’s Environmental Hearing Board.
DEP officials came to the conclusion that they should use a stricter permitting system, suspending approvals for roadspreading statewide. That didn’t stop the practice entirely, though. Although the agency banned roadspreading wastewater from fracked wells, its efforts to place similar restrictions on conventional operators failed—in large part because of the political power these companies hold in Northwestern Pennsylvania. Conventional well owners could take advantage of a loophole: Waste could be designated a “coproduct,” comparable to commercial dust-suppression products, and sold.
Lawson has continued to document trucks dumping waste, describing the oily residue the water leaves behind, which sometimes tints the roads an eerie blue. At a 2024 state Senate hearing, Karen Feridun, co-founder of the environmental advocacy organization Better Path Coalition, testified that DEP records show over 3.5 million gallons of wastewater had been dumped on Pennsylvania roads between 2018 and 2024.
The DEP submitted testimony that staff had reached out to all operators who listed roadspreading as an end use for their wastewater in 2022 and 2023. As of 2023, only two operators still actively listed roadspreading as an end use, and neither responded to the DEP’s calls to halt operations. This is likely an undercount, said Hess, “because the [conventional well] industry just does not comply with anything. I mean, DEP itself issued a report in December 2022 that said this industry has a history of non-compliance.”
An August report from FracTracker Alliance found that roughly 70 percent of Pennsylvania’s conventional oil and gas wells reported oil and gas waste production but no waste—a massive gap in regulatory oversight, said Hess. When the DEP told a company called BCD Properties that its oil and gas wastewater was invalid as a coproduct, the company filed an appeal. The case was ultimately settled privately, but two weeks before the settlement, DEP issued the new permit that opened up another loophole.
BCD Properties was initially trying to sell wastewater from its Danylko 4 well in McKean County. The new permit issued for the Danylko 6 well is roughly 500 feet away—it draws from the same geologic formation and will still bring up oil and gas—but it’s been established as a “mineral brine” well. What this means is that the company will be able to sell brine as its primary product, then sell whatever oil and gas is extracted as “waste.”
The result is “extremely concerning,” said Palladino. In order to sell their brine, operators are expected to test it and decide on their own whether it’s comparable to commercial products and meets health and human safety standards—this is called a “coproduct designation.” When DEP began looking more closely at oil and gas companies’ coproduct designations, they found that none of the waste met basic safety thresholds. .
“So now this [permit] comes along, and it creates this artificial distinction between a waste brine … [and] this new category called mineral brine, when it’s the same stuff, coming from the same formation,” said Palladino.
BCD Properties did not respond to requests for comment from Inside Climate News, nor did the Pennsylvania Independent Oil and Gas Association. The trade group said last year that DEP has long conducted analysis of roadspreading and found it safe, only to change course in recent years.

From our collaborating partner “Living on Earth,” public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by producer Aynsley O’Neill with
Plastics have been widely adopted in all sorts of products from food packaging to toys to medical devices, in part because they were believed to be chemically inert—meaning they don’t easily undergo chemical reactions when in contact with other substances.
But when it comes to microplastics, a recent study challenges that notion.
The study, published this month in the journal Nature, looked at several kinds of microplastics in a lab and found that when they came into contact with water, it essentially acted as a catalyst to create free radicals. Those are unstable molecules which in the human body are linked to inflammation and disease. Unlike larger, intact pieces of plastic, microplastics have far more surface area as compared to their volume, creating the conditions for chemical reactions to occur.
Dr. Leonardo Trasande is a pediatrician who directs the NYU Center for the Investigation of Environmental Hazards and was not part of the study. He shared his perspective on the results with us. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
AYNSLEY O’NEILL: When we say that plastic is considered chemically inert, what exactly does that mean, and what did this new study find to change our understanding of that?
LEONARDO TRASANDE: When plastic is inert in the notion of human physiology, it means it doesn’t do anything or interact with the human body. It goes, enters and leaves unseen essentially, from a human health perspective. What this study reveals is that plastic is not inert, particularly micro- and nanoplastics.
The assumption was that micro-nanoplastics don’t get transformed or cause any interaction with the human body. What this study found was that inflammation, the body’s response to a variety of exposures, was increased. The inflammation in the human body is important because it underlies many different medically important conditions, particularly cardiovascular disease—but I can think of a host of others.
To use cardiovascular disease as an analogy, we know that inflammation in the coronary arteries promotes the acceleration of plaque and ultimately, conditions like heart attack and even stroke. When we talk about oxidative stress or inflammation being increased in the human body as a result of plastic exposures, that by definition is not inert. It means that these plastics are quite biologically active. To be clear, we’re not even talking about the chemicals added to plastic materials or the chemical impurities that exist in plastic materials. This was simply focusing on one aspect of the multi-dimensional threat that’s posed by plastic to human health.
O’NEILL: Microplastics are fairly ubiquitous in the world these days, and as we were saying, they’ve already been linked to health concerns like inflammation and hormone disruption. To what extent does this research simply explain why microplastics have these effects, versus give us new health concerns to consider?
TRASANDE: If I can pick up the cardiovascular disease issue, the New England Journal of Medicine a couple years back published a study looking at the carotid artery, which is the artery that provides large amounts of blood flow to the brain, head and neck. What it found was that polyvinyl and polyethylene micro-nanoplastics, the levels in those carotid arteries—these are patients who underwent a procedure called endarterectomy to essentially clean out the carotid artery—the microplastic concentrations in those plaques were associated with a fourfold increase in the composite of heart attack, stroke and death.
So what this study does is further unravels a mechanism that may directly explain why those microplastics were associated with such a steep increase in a major human health condition.
O’NEILL: What, if anything, does this study tell us about why microplastics are acting differently than their macro counterparts?
TRASANDE: Microplastics may do one of two things: they may deliver chemicals of concern to human tissue, or they themselves can be human wrecking balls, or otherwise cause inflammation by just their interaction and physical properties. This study suggests a little bit more that the latter is the case, but it doesn’t preclude the fact that chemicals that are coming along for the ride may further exacerbate the inflammation that was observed in relationship to micro-nanoplastics.
O’NEILL: We’ve talked about a few of the health concerns here. Which one stands out to you?
TRASANDE: Well, oxidative stress and inflammation is such a common thread throughout so many human health conditions that it’s hard to pick any one. Let’s even take hormone disruption, for example. Inflammation can further contribute to endocrine disruption. Inflammation can contribute to immune dysfunction. I can go condition by condition across the lifespan, and this study indirectly reveals a link that hadn’t been previously described.
It’s not to say that microplastics are the cause of everything and anything under the sun, or not the totality of chronic disease. I’m still always going to say that diet and physical activity are important risk factors for obesity and cardiovascular disease, just to name those two. But this study adds further basis for considering a third leg to that stool, and those are environmental exposures that may be impactful.

Work has started on a project to restore 435 hectares (1,077 acres) of damaged peatland.
Cumbria Wildlife Trust will carry out the work in Skiddaw Forest where it will also repair a 6km (3.7-mile) boundary fence.
The forest is home to one of the largest continuous areas of blanket bog in the Lake District and acts as a huge carbon store.
Peatland team manager for the trust Susie Webb said: "Once improved, the peatlands will also slow the flow of water off the fells, which will help protect local communities downstream from flooding and will benefit a huge variety of wildlife."
The project is expected to take between three and four months but public access to Skiddaw Forest won't be affected.
Webb said: "We expect to see an increase in specialist plants such as sundews and sphagnum mosses and greater numbers of dragonflies.
"Birds such as snipe, which live on wet grassland, marshes and moorlands, will benefit from the rewetted ground."

17e34ba041a5.text: The governments of Washington D.C. and Virginia asked a federal court to block construction of President Trump's planned " triumphal arch ," claiming it's unlawfully tall and would snarl traffic for years. Why it matters: It's a last-minute gambit to stop construction before the multi-year project begins, potentially as soon as this coming week. What they're saying: " This project is flagrantly unlawful," the two governments said in a Saturday filing in D.C. federal court, first reported by the Washington Post. "During the three-year period of construction, the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges," they argue. They further claim that the defendants — the National Park Service and the Interior Department — have rushed the project without the proper consultations. The city and state are asking a judge to issue injunctions to stop any site preparation or construction on the project. Zoom out: The proposed 250-foot arch would be one of the largest such monuments in the world, sparking concerns that it could interfere with other national symbols, block views and even complicate landings for pilots at nearby airports. (The FAA found otherwise.) The Park Service's own August report indicated the construction of the arch would have adverse effects on nearby monuments and landmarks. The other side: The administration has argued it will be a major tourist attraction — but also vital to national security, serving as a base for snipers and drones. The White House was not immediately available to comment Saturday on the D.C. / Virginia petition. What's next: A federal judge held a hearing Friday on a separate challenge to the arch, and indicated she may block construction at least temporarily.

4d615b18f28f.text: By — Tom Nouvian, Associated Press Tom Nouvian, Associated Press By — Kirsten Grieshaber, Associated Press Kirsten Grieshaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/a-third-weekend-of-protests-in-france-as-youth-led-rallies-sweep-europe Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A third weekend of protests in France as youth-led rallies sweep Europe World Oct 31, 2026 1:14 PM EDT PARIS (AP) — Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education. About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital's edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy. READ MORE: France pledges new university admissions to quell student anger. But only after Macron leaves office France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers' turnout estimates are much higher. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a "very high risk" of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays. At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of France's largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets. The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle. A person releases colored smoke as protesters take part in a demonstration organized by labor unions as part of nationwide protests called by the "Yellow Vests" movement joined by French high school and university students against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in Paris on Oct. 31, 2026. Photo by Abdul Saboor/Reuters The marchers' grievances are diverse. Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living. A few Halloween costumes stood out in the crowd, including a zombie Michael Jackson from "Thriller," a pirate and a Spider-Man. Protesters waited calmly, chanting and singing through megaphones. Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where "there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats." He said that he hoped Saturday's protest would be festive in honor of Halloween, to counter the image of violence that has attached itself to France's protests. Police impose curfew and other measures The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands. While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting — including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries. WATCH: Why French students are leading massive protests across the country Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday. Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement. Protests are also taking place in Germany, Italy and Spain In Germany, a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" — roughly "Gen Z's got this" — rallied in many cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that more than 180,000 people had signed up online, but as of Saturday afternoon only several thousand marched in various cities across the country. Young protesters also gathered at Berlin's Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing. "We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection — in short, in our future — because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said. Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education. "At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said. A heart-shaped balloon with the word "Revolution" floats into the sky during a demonstration organized by labor unions as part of nationwide protests called by the "Yellow Vests" movement, joined by French high school and university students against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in Marseille, France, on Oct. 31, 2026. Photo by Manon Cruz/Reute

b9799cdc3f1c.text: By — Amy Sherman, PolitiFact Amy Sherman, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/when-will-we-know-2026-midterm-election-results-it-may-take-some-time-but-thats-normal Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter When will we know 2026 midterm election results? It may take some time, but that's normal Politics Oct 31, 2026 1:02 PM EDT This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. If you go to bed on election night and don't know who won a midterm congressional race, that's normal. And if you wake up the next morning and find that a candidate who was behind hours earlier has since pulled ahead, that's normal, too. That won't stop some politicians and their allies from spreading misinformation during vote counting. WATCH: How does The Associated Press call 2026 midterm election winners? 4 things to know In past elections, elected leaders, candidates and social media users have spread falsehoods that "late night" arrivals of "ballot dumps" or "suitcases" of ballots are signs of fraud, or that only Democratic-led cities take days to count votes. Some states such as Florida often complete the majority of their unofficial counts in fewer hours or days than elsewhere. But it is not a sign of fraud if other places need more time. "States are neither fast or slow, they all count and certify the results in accordance with the laws passed by their state legislature," said Ryan Macias, an election technology and cybersecurity expert. "What is fast or slow is how quickly the media can collect sufficient evidence to confidently predict the winner, which is typically based on the margin of victory." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Voters can help elections run smoothly. People who vote by mail, for instance, should not wait until the last minute to submit their ballots. Many election offices provide secure drop boxes to speed the return of mailed ballots. The U.S. Postal Service recommends that voters mail in their ballot at least one week before the deadline. "There are always a handful of really close Senate and House races in which the winner will not be determined for several days or, in the cases of Alaska and California, as much as a week or two," said Joe Lenski, executive vice president of SSRS, which conducts a national exit poll on Election Day. Control of the U.S. Senate could come down to a handful of close races with large numbers of ballots to count. No state is required to complete the official count on election night. State laws set deadlines to certify final results, often weeks later. Here's a look at what could influence the timing of unofficial results. Close margins Polls and nonpartisan analysis show many U.S. Senate races are competitive, including in Michigan, Maine, Iowa, Alaska, Kansas and Texas. If the counts are close in the first few hours or even days after polls close, media outlets may have to wait for officials to count more ballots until journalists can project a winner. Some close races could end in a recount completed days or weeks later. In 2018, three Florida statewide races were settled in recounts. Candidates who lead early in the vote count may not ultimately win. In 2020, Donald Trump was up by more than 100,000 votes in Wisconsin early in the night, but the picture quickly shifted after Milwaukee's central count finished processing mail-in votes around 3:30 a.m local time. The late boost for Joe Biden from Milwaukee was expected, especially because Wisconsin's mail-in ballots tend to skew Democratic. The pattern of when votes are counted — and what political leanings those jurisdictions' voters tend to have — varies by state. Mail ballot volume and receipt deadlines It takes time to process mail ballots. Election workers must verify voter identity, for example, by matching envelope signatures against registration records. Most states, including Florida, require that mail ballots be received by Election Day. But some states allow voters to return ballots later as long as they were postmarked by Election Day. In California, which runs nearly all-mail elections, ballots postmarked by Election Day and received up to a week later are permitted. The U.S. Supreme Court in June upheld the right of states to have such a policy, a blow to Trump, who says he wants a faster process and has spread falsehoods about California's vote counting. READ MORE: 5 expert takeaways on 2026 midterm election security Ohio passed a law in 2025 that said most absentee ballots must be received by the close of polls on Election Day; previously it had a four-day grace period. In California, counties must count and report the results from most ballots by the 13th day after the election. There are some exceptions to that, including for provisional ballots and mail ballots with signature verification needs; election officials should be done counting those within 30 days after the election. In U.S. House races, there are always a handful of districts that are not called on election night or the day after, mostly in California, Lenski said. Last minute absentee ballot submissions: A Michigan case study When thousands of voters procrastinate sending in their mail ballots until the last minute, it takes election workers extra time to process and count those ballots. In past elections, some people have spread falsehoods about such "delays" in places like Detroit, pointing to vans with ballots arriving late at night as evidence of foul play. The winner of the U.S. Senate race may not be clear until officials can count nearly all of Detroit's ballots. Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.
The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.
Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.
It said it had replenished the assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.
The company said its next goal is resuming withdrawal services for users, saying it remained on track to reopen withdrawals on Sunday 1 November and would provide a further update once details were confirmed.
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025.
Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".
Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners.
The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group called The Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor, as the likely culprits.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange last year.
North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

140f1fccca21.text: By — Ope Adetayo, Associated Press Ope Adetayo, Associated Press By — Constant Same Bagalwa, Associated Press Constant Same Bagalwa, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/congos-ebola-deaths-top-5000-as-fear-of-continent-wide-spread-mounts Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Congo's Ebola deaths top 5,000 as fear of continent-wide spread mounts World Oct 31, 2026 11:25 AM EDT BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Deaths in Congo's Ebola outbreak have topped 5,000 as the country grapples with the relentless spread of the disease and cases are recorded in other African countries, the latest government data on Saturday shows. Data from the Congolese Ministry of Health showed that the disease has killed 5,026 people out of 10,351 infected, at a nearly 50% lethality rate. The surge is sparking concerns among experts regarding the authorities' ability to contain the deadly virus. The latest outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, was declared in mid-May, catching authorities by surprise. They have since struggled to manage it. READ MORE: 1st confirmed Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland It is already the second deadliest Ebola outbreak in history, second only to a two-year-long West Africa outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people across multiple countries. "It is a very tragic milestone because it is just not a number," said Dr. Patrick Otim, a programme area manager with the World Health Organization. "It is families and communities that have been devastated by this outbreak. The number also shows the severity of this outbreak." 2,788 people have recovered from the virus so far. The Bundibugyo virus has no known vaccine or treatment, but health workers treat patients based on symptoms. One-third of people who have died did not get to receive any care Since May, the disease has spread to 67 out of the country's 178 health zones in eight of 26 provinces. Fifty of the affected 67 health zones have active cases. The virus has been concentrated in the eastern region of Congo, especially in Ituri and North Kivu, which have emerged as the epicenters with 9,782 total confirmed cases and 4,792 total deaths. Authorities are still struggling with tracing contacts and testing, key components in the race to curb the outbreak. READ MORE: Nigeria confirms Ebola case in its capital as woman who arrived from Uganda tests positive According to the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about 80% of new cases are coming from outside the chain of monitored contacts, meaning an overwhelming share of infections are coming from unknown chains of transmission to health authorities. Also, one-third of recorded deaths are victims who have died outside of treatment centers, before being tested for Ebola, WHO's Otim said. These issues, health officials say, contribute to community transmission outside of the immediate purview of health workers who can effectively manage infection in accordance with medical protocols. "These are people we never had opportunity to try to save them and it is one of the biggest concerns for us in this outbreak. How do we try to reach people early to get them to come to health facilities to get a fighting chance to survive?" Otim said. 'The outbreak is stretching everyone responding to it' The explosive number of infections in Congo comes on the heels of a long list of issues that have hamstrung efforts to contain the outbreak. The eastern region of Congo, where the outbreak is concentrated, plays host to a conflict between the government and an array of armed groups, most prominently the Rwanda-backed M23 rebel group, and there is also an Islamist insurgency in the border areas with Uganda, where the Allied Democratic Forces carry out attacks, limiting the reach of healthcare workers. Also, there is widespread disbelief among the population, which has led to a series of attacks on health workers and health facilities. A nurse was killed while responding to an Ebola alert last week, and a politician from the ruling party was killed in September after advocating for health measures on the radio. Health workers have gone on multiple strikes, shutting down facilities where they treat infected people, citing long delays in payments by the government. On Friday, workers at an Ebola treatment center in Tchomia, in Ituri, downed tools, demanding four months of unpaid wages. At the center, there are currently five confirmed Ebola patients and 10 suspected cases under care. READ MORE: Congo's confirmed Ebola cases surpass 9,000 as containment efforts falter "We are tired of requesting our salaries. If they want to pay us, they will. ... Today, being able to feed our families has become a real problem," Moise Mugenyi, one of the striking workers, told the AP. Dr. Justin Mukonkole, acting head of response operations in Ituri, said the workers should be patient while the government responds to their demands. Similar situations have played out in other health zones like Beni in North Kivu, where services in some treatment centers have ground to a halt. Alain Siwako, an elected public official in Beni, said cases are spiralling in Beni because of a lack of fuel and financial resources from the central government. "Across Ituri and North Kivu, this outbreak is stretching everyone responding to it, including the communities themselves," Rose Tchwenko, Country Director for the DRC, Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said. In October, both Kenya and Nigeria confirmed cases of Ebola. Kenya has confirmed eight cases and 2 deaths, while Nigeria's sole confirmed case had been evacuated to Switzerland. The confirmation of cases in both countries, and earlier in Uganda, made the latest outbreak the first recorded in three African regions and the continent's most geographically widespread outbreak. Ope Adetayo reported from Lagos, Nigeria. The Associated Press receives financial support for global health and

More than 5,000 people have died from an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, government data shows.
Eight of 26 provinces are now affected, with more than 10,300 confirmed cases.
The outbreak, which started in May, became the country's deadliest in its history in August, public health officials said. The current case fatality rate is 48.6%.
In its latest update, the health ministry said the epicentre of the epidemic remains in the Ituri province, in the north-east of the country, which is a conflict zone, making it harder to contain the virus.
Cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
This marks the 17th outbreak in DR Congo's history, according to the United Nations (UN), and the second largest in history.
The World Health Organization (WHO) office in Africa said a "continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach" is needed to end the outbreak.
Testing and treatment are under way, along with clinical trials of vaccines, it added.
The Bundibugyo species is behind the current outbreak, but there is not yet any treatment or vaccine for this strain.
DR Congo's previous deadliest outbreak saw 2,299 deaths recorded between 2018-2020, the UN said.
The deadliest in history occurred in West Africa between 2014 and 2016, killing more than 11,325 people and spread across several countries, including Italy, the UK and United States, according to the WHO.
The UN warns that the current outbreak is "taking lives at a much faster rate".
Ebola is a rare, deadly disease caused by a virus, and symptoms come on suddenly.
As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Adding to the challenge of treating the disease, some health workers and a politician have been attacked while responding to the outbreak.
Earlier this week, a nurse was killed and another health worker seriously injured in an attack when responding to an Ebola alert. Local youths had accused them of contaminating water sources and spreading the virus, according to the UN-backed Radio Okapi.
Last month, a politician was beaten to death after promoting measures to stop the spread of Ebola, while in August, the Red Cross said its volunteers had been injured and an ambulance set on fire in 11 violent incidents in the outbreak's first 100 days.
In Uganda, two people died and 20 cases were recorded shortly after the outbreak started, but no cases have been reported since August. Travel restrictions remain in place for those crossing into the country from neighbouring DR Congo.
In Kenya, there have been nine confirmed cases and two recorded deaths.
Two suspected cases were identified in Nigeria on Saturday, its disease control centre said, adding that the individuals have been isolated and they are undergoing testing.
Earlier in October, one woman was confirmed to have the disease in the country but was flown to Switzerland for further treatment.
The likelihood of infection for people in the Europe area is "very low," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said.

f87bc9ac4915.text: By — Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press By — Chan Ho-him, Associated Press Chan Ho-him, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/what-to-know-about-the-6-3b-hack-on-binance-likely-the-biggest-ever-crypto-theft Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft World Oct 31, 2026 11:14 AM EDT Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. Blockchain firms have pointed to the attack coming from a North Korean hacking unit. The company said it has reserved more than $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the stolen assets and was beginning to recover assets for users. Binance worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. WATCH: $6 billion cryptocurrency heist puts investors on edge The cryptocurrency exchange has promised to cover all losses, and it has been sharing regular updates on its social media channels as it uncovers more information about the hack. "We are working nonstop to resolve this," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said Friday in a video posted to X. In an exchange Friday with reporters at the White House, President Donald Trump said U.S. officials were investigating the Binance hack. Asked whether North Korea was involved, Trump said: "We're looking at that." Here's what we know about the hack, possible North Korean involvement and Binance's investigation. North Korean hackers are suspected in the attack Binance said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach." U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM, in a post on its website late Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said. "An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists." Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice." Experts have said that North Korea turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities in recent years as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties. In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets over the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the world's best. Many are calling this the biggest crypto theft on record While about half of the stolen assets were frozen, there is evidence that the hackers already are transferring and converting some of what wasn't recovered, said Garrick Hileman, an independent cryptocurrency analyst. "Like in money laundering, you bring in the stolen goods and launder those through a mixer or tumbler," he said. "You mix it in with other cryptos, and it's harder to track." How long it will take the hackers to turn that into something usable isn't clear, he said. "The bottom line is there are places in the world where you can take your bitcoin and get that converted," Hileman said. READ MORE: Binance flags 'potential security issue,' says approximately $6.3 billion impacted TRM and several other crypto firms and experts have said the hack represents the largest cryptocurrency theft on record. In February of last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack. TRM listed the Bybit hack when it referenced similarities between the Binance hack and previous attacks linked to TraderTraitor. Binance's founder, Changpeng Zhao, wrote on X that while Binance's hack might be the largest in terms of its dollar value, previous attacks on other companies like the crypto exchange Mt. Gox have had a more substantial impact in terms of the bitcoin amount affected, he said. Experts warn this scale of hacking could become more commonplace. "A cyber attack of this level is a matter of when, not if, particularly alongside the rise of AI," said Andy Ward, a senior vice president at Absolute Security. "Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines." Where experts — and Binance — say things went wrong The hack has raised questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, co-founder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab. "This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and that are connected to the internet. Teng, Binance's co-CEO, confirmed in a nearly five-minute video posted on X Friday that Binance's own hot wallet was affected. "User assets are held under Binance's established security architecture," he said. "The vast majority sits in cold wallets" — which are offline and used for secure storage — "and are only moved into a hot walle

The civilians traveled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus, following a deal brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump. Ukrainian authorities imposed restrictions on disclosing the number of evacuees or the border crossing location. The measures are to safeguard those who chose to remain in Oleshky as well as to protect future humanitarian missions, the organizers said. READ MORE: Aid operation and evacuations in Oleshky amid brief truce agreed to by Russia and Ukraine The ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, which began at 3 a.m. Tuesday, is expected to continue through Sunday evening. The estimated 2,000 remaining residents of Oleshky were offered the choice of traveling to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. Those who chose to return to Ukraine were taken to the Russian city of Anapa then flown to Homel in Belarus, from where they proceeded back home. Daughters wait to see their fathers again Relatives waited on Saturday at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border, along with aid tents, coffee stands and even provisions to feed the pets the evacuees were bringing with them. Volunteers from organizations, including the Red Cross, Doctors without Borders and the World Central Kitchen, were also there. Liza Paliy, 19, who last saw her father over 2½ years ago when she, her mother and sister fled from the occupied territory while he stayed behind, was among those waiting. "We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately, two years have already passed," she said. Daria Pavlyn also waited at the border in hopes of reuniting with her father, Mykhailo, whom she had not heard from in about a month. He had planned to flee occupied territory with his family after a nearby strike killed two neighbors but stayed behind when arrangements to care for the family's home and animals fell through. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has put his cabinet ministers and other senior government officials through military training, saying armed forces discipline can help build stronger leaders and advance the country's development.
Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre.
The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training.
Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba.
It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last.
In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable.
He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership.
"Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both.
Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives.
The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia.
It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries.
Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions.

Environmental campaigners have staged a Halloween themed demonstration outside the first minister's official residence over "scary" fossil fuels.
Climate groups gathered outside Bute House in Edinburgh to protest against the Scottish government's decision to give the go-ahead for a new, gas-fired, power station at Peterhead in Aberdeenshire.
The decision has been branded a "catastrophic failure" by environmental campaigners, who said burning fossil fuels is the key driver of extreme weather such as recent storms, record heat and flooding.
The Scottish government said it remained committed to tackling climate change.
The protest also comes after the announcement from the UK government that the Jackdaw gas field near Aberdeen would be allowed to go ahead.
Protesters wearing Halloween themed masks and holding placards with messages such as "fossil fuel ghouls" and "this decision will haunt you" gathered on Charlotte Square.
Kate Whitaker of Friends of the Earth Scotland said fossil fuels are "scary" because of the harm they are causing "millions of people".
"When politicians make disastrous decisions to approve new oil or gas, people get even more terrified about our collective future," she said.
"Giving the go ahead for a new fossil-fuelled power plant at Peterhead is a catastrophic failure from the Scottish government to protect people from both climate breakdown and the increasing burden of household energy bills.
"Politicians could instead help allay our fears by focusing on climate solutions that improve people's lives such as warmer homes, reliable bus services and creating green jobs."
A Scottish government spokesperson said: "We remain unwavering in our commitment to tackle climate change, delivering positive climate action to achieve net zero by 2045.
"The full grounds for the ministers' decision are set out in the decision letter.
"Potential impacts on communities, nature and cultural heritage, including the cumulative effects of developments, were important considerations in the decision-making process."

5c6a9f87a89a.text: You won't need to stay up all night Tuesday to spot a big Democratic wave in the 2026 midterm elections . But it could take days — or even weeks — to know whether Republicans have survived a smaller one and held on to the House or Senate. Why it matters: A handful of early results in key states and congressional districts will tell us whether Democrats are headed for a landslide or disappointment. What we're watching: Florida, Florida, Florida. Most polls close at 7pm ET, and the state counts quickly — ready for release when the Panhandle finally calls it a night an hour later. At 8:01pm , refresh your browser and watch FL-14. The great mid-cycle redistricting wars transformed this Tampa-based district from Harris +8 to Trump +11. If Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor survives, Republicans can all but kiss their majority goodbye, according to party strategists. Next up is FL-25. The country's most expensive general election race is playing out in a district that went from Harris +4 to Trump +9. If Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz's race is close — or too close to call early in the night — House Republicans can keep hope alive. While you're at it, this is a good time to check on South Carolina's Senate race, where polls close at 7pm and the state counts relatively fast. If Sen. Darline Graham loses to Annie Andrews in the Trump +18 state, Senate Republicans can say goodbye to their majority. (And they'll be sweating if it's close.) "Underperformance is rarely isolated," said Jason Thielman, executive director of the National Republican Senatorial Committee in 2024. "If you see the GOP underperforming early in the East, it is likely going to continue as you move further West." At 9pm, check in on Virginia: The commonwealth's polls close at 7pm, but historically tight races often aren't called until the 9pm hour. If Democrats flip VA-01, a Trump +5 seat, they're in for a very good night. If they flip VA-05, a Trump +12 seat, they're in for a great night. Between the lines: VA-02 could tell us whether a strong Republican candidate can survive a Democratic wave, and whether Speaker Mike Johnson can keep his job. Trump carried the Hampton Roads district by just 0.2 percentage points in 2024, while Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans won by 3.8 points. The AP didn't call her race until 5:28pm ET the following Wednesday. GOP strategists believe Kiggans has run a nearly flawless campaign. If even she gets swept away in a 50-50 district, other Republicans in a low-single-digit Trump seat should brace for impact. If she holds on, that could bode well for Sen. Susan Collins in Maine and Rep. Ashley Hinson in the Iowa Senate race. The intrigue: Also keep an eye on Kentucky's 6th District. Polls close there at 6pm ET, but the state takes a more genteel approach to counting ballots. If Democrats take the open Lexington-based seat (Trump +15), Republicans will be downing their bourbon. Neat. Moving west: Polls close in Ohio at 7:30pm and Texas at 8pm ET, but Texas counts faster. If Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton holds on, Republicans still have a path to keeping their Senate majority. Iowa polls close at 9pm ET. If Hinson is looking good, the night might not be as bad as many Republicans feared. The bottom line: Don't stay up for the Senate results in either Maine or Alaska. Even a clear win (or defeat) for Collins may not be obvious until Wednesday. In 2020, when she won by nearly 9 percentage points, the AP didn't call the race until lunchtime Wednesday. In Alaska, with its ranked-choice voting, results could take weeks.

5579866f60d4.text: By — Dave Collins, Associated Press Dave Collins, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-dismisses-trump-suit-against-wall-street-journal-over-epstein-birthday-letter Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge dismisses Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letter Politics Oct 31, 2026 5:32 PM EDT Saying the president was "grasping at straws," a federal judge on Saturday threw out Donald Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a story reporting on his ties to wealthy financier Jeffrey Epstein. U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed the suit with prejudice, ruling that the president did not prove the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice as required by law. The ruling said the lawsuit had attempted to "manufacture" flaws in the Journal's investigative reporting. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. When a case is thrown out "with prejudice," it cannot be refiled again and the dismissal is permanent and incontrovertible. The dismissal is a blow to Trump and his administration, which have both pursued adversarial relationships with news organizations during his second term. In addition to the Journal, he is embroiled in lawsuits involving the BBC, The Associated Press and — most recently — CNN, MS NOW and Politico, which are suing him for restored access after he banished them from the White House in mid-September. Trump has denounced media outlets that write things to which he objects and frequently calls them "fake news" and insults their journalists. Trump called the reporting 'malicious' The lawsuit against the Journal was over a story it published last year describing a sexually suggestive letter and drawing that the paper said bore Trump's name and was included in a 2003 album compiled for Epstein's 50th birthday. The letter was reportedly collected by disgraced British socialite Ghislaine Maxwell as part of a birthday album for Epstein years before he was first arrested in 2006 and subsequently had a falling-out with Trump. The letter bearing Trump's name includes text framed by the outline of what appears to be a hand-drawn naked woman and ends with, "Happy Birthday — and may every day be another wonderful secret," according to the newspaper. READ MORE: Trump mired in Epstein controversy as Wall Street Journal reports on 2003 letter Trump denied writing it and called the story "false, malicious, and defamatory." The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Miami, accused the paper and its reporters of having "knowingly and recklessly" published "numerous false, defamatory, and disparaging statements," which, it alleged, caused "overwhelming financial and reputational harm" to the president. The suit was dismissed once, then refiled Gayles previously dismissed the suit in April, saying Trump had failed to make the argument that the article was published with the intent to be malicious. But he gave the president a chance to file an amended complaint, which he did in May. In Saturday's ruling, the judge cited the Supreme Court's landmark 1964 ruling in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. That decision made it harder for public figures to win libel lawsuits because it requires proof that a media outlet knowingly published something false or showed a reckless disregard for the truth. READ MORE: Trump sues Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over story reporting on Epstein ties "The Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice," Gayles wrote. "Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false." The judge also noted that the Journal's story did not ignore or minimize Trump's denial, "Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it." Gayles also said several other allegations in the lawsuit did not have merit. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across Europe
Hundreds of thousands of protesters demonstrated across France as the country prepares for a general strike in the coming days.
In Paris, police fired tear gas and clashed with protesters in a third weekend of nationwide demonstrations against the rising cost of living and poor public services.
More than 320,000 people took to the streets around the country and at least 290 protesters were arrested, according to France's interior ministry. Police say about 70,000 demonstrated in Paris.
The authorities prepared extensively to avoid a repeat of the violence, rioting and looting that happened two weeks ago.
Protests also took place in Albania, Germany and Italy as youth take to the streets across Europe, the BBC's correspondent James Waterhouse reports.

bbc546ea5784.text: A federal judge on Saturday threw out President Trump's lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over the paper's reporting on Trump's ties to Jeffrey Epstein, Why it matters: It's the second time this year courts have blocked Trump's efforts to sue the paper over stories about his relationship with the disgraced financier. As with the first one, courts found the president did not clear the high bar set by New York Times vs. Sullivan for allegations of defamation in critical reporting on public figures. Driving the news: Judge Darrin Gayles of the southern district of Florida issued the 20-page ruling Saturday afternoon, finding that Trump failed to prove the paper acted with "actual malice" by reporting on his links to Epstein. Gayles dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice, meaning it can't be refiled. Zoom out: Trump first filed suit against the paper and Murdoch in July 2025, seeking $20 billion in damages. At issue was a story describing a "bawdy" letter, bearing Trump's name and given to Epstein for his birthday, which the president insisted was fake. Gayles tossed the initial suit last April, but allowed Trump to file an amended complaint — which was the one he dismissed Saturday, saying it fell short of the burden to prove the paper acted maliciously. What they're saying: "Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false," Gayles wrote. For the record: " President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants. The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions," a spokesman for his legal team said in a statement. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details. Sara Fischer contributed.

f02fdd11cf95.text: By — Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/analysis-more-than-40-of-names-on-doj-list-of-alleged-noncitizens-not-on-californias-voter-rolls Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Analysis: More than 40% of names on DOJ list of alleged noncitizens not on California's voter rolls Politics Updated on Oct 31, 2026 5:20 PM EDT — Published on Oct 31, 2026 4:03 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — More than 4 in 10 names flagged as possible noncitizen voters in California by the Trump administration cannot be found on the state's voter rolls, according to a legal filing Saturday by an immigrant-rights group. It's the first outside analysis of a list that the Department of Justice has used to threaten prosecution of election officials. The analysis also found that thousands of U.S. citizens appear to be flagged as ineligible to vote on the government's list. Please check your inbox to confirm. The contention was made in a filing by two data analysts at the University of California, Los Angeles. They analyzed the 20,930 names that the department demanded that California election officials treat as possible illegal voters by separating their ballots during the vote count on Election Day. Multiple judges have rejected the demand as unconstitutional and a threat to democracy, and local and state officials have said the list appears riddled with errors. Court filing outlines problems with government list The breadth of the problems with the list was outlined in Saturday's filing. It describes an analysis by two members of UCLA's Voting Rights Project, who filed a lawsuit challenging it with the Los Angeles-based Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA. The research found that 8,880 of the names, representing 42% of the entire list, do not correspond to anyone in California's current voter file. It also found at least 22 are U.S. citizens, and many more may correspond to those of confirmed citizens. "The expert analysis further makes clear that the mandated voter list endangers a significant number of eligible California voter," said the filing, which was cosigned by Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for California governor and an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project. The Trump administration had objected to sharing the list, calling it a "fishing expedition" and noting that it included sensitive information. In a social media post, Trump claimed his Justice Department found "20,000, but potentially Hundreds of Thousands, and maybe even Millions," of fraudulent votes, "and the Court has just ruled against it. Why would they reject fixing Election Fraud?" The Trump administration has also urged Washington state to remove what it says were 400 possible noncitizens on its rolls, though state election officials there say that list is also unreliable and includes one voter who cast ballots in the 1990s. The Justice Department has also warned California election officials they could face criminal liability if they let noncitizens vote and issued subpoenas of election offices there. Election officials say they have no time to investigate Election officials have complained that the Trump administration has confronted them with lists of possible illegal voters at the last minute before Election Day, with no time to conduct the painstaking investigation required by law before removing someone from the rolls. Multiple lawsuits have been filed to stop the administration from continuing to threaten local election officials. READ MORE: How some states are responding to DOJ's plan to send 1,000 monitors on Election Day On Friday, a federal judge in California ordered the Justice Department to stop sending demands to state officials, a decision the Trump administration appealed Saturday. Several counties in the state had run quick checks of the Trump list and found numerous errors. Saturday's broader analysis was possible because a federal judge on Friday ordered the Trump administration to share the list with the plaintiffs in the case. CHIRLA and the UCLA project sued the Homeland Security Department in early October to prevent it from using federal immigration data to challenge state voter rolls. The lawsuit cited examples in other states where the federal government's data has been proven to mistakenly include thousands of citizens. Case argues that government's methods pose risk to voting The case argued that the data-matching methods risk disenfranchising or deterring citizens from voting. On top of that, plaintiffs argued, the lists could disproportionately target naturalized citizens who are legally entitled to vote. Applying the government's methodology, the UCLA researchers found that nearly 7,500 naturalized citizens in the state were "highly likely" to be incorrectly flagged as ineligible. They described the voter ID number as the most crucial data point. The Justice Department argues that there is just as much to lose if the ballots aren't separated. Sullivan donor in candidate's hometown as Alaska Senate inquiry widens Politics Oct 31, 2026 3:50 PM EDT ANCHORAGE, Alaska (AP) — The FBI has begun reaching out to donors of Dan J. Sullivan asking about potential deception, as federal authorities ramped up their investigation of the U.S. Senate candidate in Alaska who shares a name with the Republican incumbent. An Anchorage-based FBI agent visited a boat dealership in Petersburg, a small fishing community accessible only by air or water where the candidate lives. Flint said the FBI agent asked his son, who works at the dealership, whether Flint felt he had been "misled" about which candidate he was supporting.
