Olha has one word to describe what life has been like in the front-line city of Oleshky over the past few years: "Horror".
Disembarking alongside her from a coach in the Ukrainian region of Chernihiv with their immediate family and dog, her husband Viacheslav put it this way: "We came back from hell."
The couple were among hundreds of residents evacuated from the Russian-occupied city who crossed into northern Ukraine via Belarus on Saturday, many reuniting with loved ones they had not seen for years.
Oleshky, seized by Russia during the first few days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, is trapped on one side by the Dnipro River and on the other side by Russian forces.
Olha and Viacheslav had lived there with their son and daughter, both in their 30s. Even as the shelling around them intensified, they feared that trying to escape could be even more dangerous, with routes mined and subject to drone attack.
As supplies dwindled, the couple said they made an attempt to find food by crossing through minefields earlier this month. "People were stepping on mines, dying and being maimed, all just to survive," Olha told the BBC.
Those who were too afraid to go out in the city had resorted to cooking garden weeds to survive.
"We saw that the situation wasn't getting any better, so we realised we had to get out," Olha said.
That opportunity came earlier this week when a humanitarian ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, took effect in the Kherson region, providing the first few days of peace in the area for four years and allowing Oleshky residents to evacuate.
Up to 6,000 people, including 200 children, were believed to still be living in Oleshky and its surrounding areas, with 1,700 in the city itself.
Residents had a four-hour window on Friday to leave, with a convoy of 25 buses brought in for up to 750 evacuees, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
After travelling through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, then flying to Belarus, evacuees arrived on buses to a military facility in Chernihiv on Saturday.
On the tarmac, where evacuees were processed before travelling onwards, some elderly residents were so weak they had to be carried on stretchers.
For many, there were emotional reunions.
As Mykhailo Palii arrived, his daughters Dasha and Anya, who thought they might never see him again, sprinted across the tarmac screaming and crying.
After an emotional embrace, Palii described a glimpse of life in Oleshky, although he said he had, until then, kept many of the details from his family.
"A hole was blown into the bathroom," he said. "There were drone attacks and missile strikes. It happened, but I didn't tell them about it because I knew they would worry."
Tetiana and Volodymyr, a couple carrying a cat when they arrived in Chernihiv, said their entire home was burned down three years ago, and they had been living in the abandoned house of a neighbour since.
For them, leaving as soon as it was safe to do so was an easy decision. "There's nothing for us to regret leaving. We don't have relatives there. Our children are married and don't live with us in the city," said Tetiana.
But those who managed to escape also worry about those left behind. "There are still a lot of people left there, living under those conditions," said Olha.
Now that the evacuees have left Oleshky, they will also face a new challenge - working out where to go next and how to rebuild their lives.
Palii said he would look for a job so he can provide for his family: "There's no job I can't handle. Digging, hoeing, planting, building. I can even do demolition work."
Olha said she and her family have no relatives elsewhere in Ukraine, and they will stay with some acquaintances for an extended period while they get back on their feet.
"If we managed to survive in hell, we'll survive here too."

6632bb6b09b6.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/virginia-and-d-c-sue-over-trumps-arch-adding-to-legal-challenges-as-government-wants-work-to-begin Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Virginia and D.C. sue over Trump's arch, adding to legal challenges as government wants work to begin Politics Updated on Oct 31, 2026 5:24 PM EDT — Published on Oct 31, 2026 2:29 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — The legal challenges to President Donald Trump's proposed memorial arch are mounting, with the District of Columbia and Virginia suing in federal court Saturday as the administration says construction could begin as early as next week. READ MORE: 2 Trump attempts to change the D.C. landscape play out in the courts as midterms near There are now three lawsuits calling for a halt to potential work on a monument that would rise 250 feet (76 meters) on a patch of grass off the bridge that spans the Potomac River, connecting the city with Arlington National Cemetery. That would make the arch 100 feet taller (30 meters) than the Statue of Liberty is from its base to the top of the torch. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan is already considering issuing an order to halt the project until the original lawsuit against the Trump administration by three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian is resolved. She held a hearing Friday but did not immediately act, though she said she would move expeditiously. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. In the latest lawsuit, two attorneys general, Brian Schwalb of Washington and Jay Jones of Virginia, argue that "as soon as Defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm on both the District and Virginia. The Arch site sits at the center of a major traffic artery between the District and Virginia, in the monumental core of the capital, on an island that straddles the Potomac River. During the three-year period of construction, the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges." As the original plaintiffs have, they also are seeking a temporary restraining order that would slow the administration's plans to move ahead imminently with construction. "The Triumphal Arch in Memorial Circle is going to be one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world," said White House spokesman Davis Ingle in an email. "It will serve as a gateway to Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike, serving as a visual reminder of the noble sacrifices borne by so many American heroes throughout our 250 year history so we can enjoy our freedoms today." The lawsuit raises concerns about how the traffic interruption would impact emergency responses in a region where joint operations are the norm, including the January 2025 midair collision between a military helicopter and airliner that killed 67. Administration wants to get started on construction The Republican administration, in a recent court filing, said it had plans to seek final approval of the project, a Trump-favorite, at Thursday's meeting of the National Capital Planning Commission and possibly begin construction the same day, despite the then-two active lawsuits pending. On Friday, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck with views to the east and west, an "occupied roof" and two mezzanines. Inside the arch are rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a "fire command center." The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national security function. Chutkan asked what the urgency was and how would the government be harmed "apart from the executive's desire to bedazzle the city" if she issues a preliminary injunction while the lawsuit plays out. Administration lawyer Robert Stander said the arch was "absolutely a high priority project" and were Chutkan to step in, that would impede the work of the government. Golf course and Kennedy Center projects also have wound up in court The lawsuits are among several that have been filed against the government as Trump seeks to remake the nation's capital at breakneck speed, prompting judges and plaintiffs to balk. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said Friday she would open a "formal inquiry" to investigate if federal attorneys violated ethical boundaries, including making misrepresentations to the court, during a legal dispute about the East Potomac Golf Link project. Trump wants the public course overhauled so it could host professional tournaments. READ MORE: Judge asked to compel Trump administration to disclose emails and texts about Kennedy Center plans There is a hearing Tuesday before U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper on a motion from Rep. Joyce Beatty, D-Ohio, an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, seeking the release of communications between the center's management and administration officials. The government has refused so far, citing executive privilege. Trump is the board chair. Beatty alleged in a separate filing Friday that the government withheld information from trustees, including an analysis from the construction manager, that would have shown that a closure was not necessary. She is challenging a govern

Emotional reunions with loved ones for Oleshky evacuees
People evacuated from the devastated Russian-occupied city of Oleshky were reunited with their loved ones after crossing from Belarus into Ukraine on Saturday.
This comes as a ceasefire brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump took effect across the frontline region of Kherson on Tuesday.
Families were reunited at a site in the region of Chernihiv in northern Ukraine after arriving in buses and ambulances.
They had previously travelled via Crimea and Russia after their evacuation from the Ukrainian town on Friday.
Ceasefire measures will remain in place until the end of Sunday 1 November.
The BBC's Dan Johnson reports from the site in the Chernihiv region, near the northern Ukrainian border with Belarus.

When they met in northern Serbia last November, Serbian President Aleksandar VuÄiÄ and Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor OrbÃ¡n could hardly have guessed they would both be out of power within a year.
Both were ousted by popular movements - OrbÃ¡n fell first, in April, defeated by PÃ©ter Magyar's Tisza party. Then last Sunday a student movement less than two years old won Serbia's parliamentary elections by a landslide.
The Tisza party in Hungary and the Student List in Serbia look very different - Tisza is centred on the personality and energy of its leader, while the students in Serbia insist they have no leadership.
But the huge turnout - 79% in Hungary and 69% in Serbia, was driven by tech-savvy young people in both countries. They used AI tools to crunch numbers, identify threats to the vote, and mobilise tens of thousands of election monitors to prevent intimidation and electoral fraud by the governing parties.
Mobilisation of voters, and the role of election monitors, played a big role in the opposition victory in both countries.
Last weekend, the DE civic action group in Hungary sent 70 election monitors to Serbia, to work with students' movement representatives, visiting polling stations in the northern Serbian province of Vojvodina.
During the summer, even before the election was called, they held workshops to share their experience and methods from the Hungarian election with the Serbian students.
A key technique was to identify "infected" polling districts in advance - places where the surprisingly high number of votes for the governing party at previous elections suggested that voter intimidation or "chain voting" techniques were used.
"From around 16:00 on election day, we noticed groups of masked hooligans - VuÄiÄ supporters - gathering near voting stations," PÃ©ter Klemm, a student activist from Subotica, told the BBC. "So we sent mobile teams, and started filming everything."
Combined with the "stationary" monitors already in place, 20 to 30 volunteers at each threatened polling station acted as a strong deterrent, he believes, and prevented intimidation or fraud.
OrbÃ¡n in Hungary, VuÄiÄ in Serbia, both looked invincible. Both were powerful leaders, in office for 16 and 14 years, who had taken over state institutions and established business empires overlapping the two countries.
Orban chose cheese, VuÄiÄ meat, when they sat down to a quick lunch of traditional burek pastries at a small, popular town centre bakery in Subotica almost a year ago.
They continued to a local winery, to talk about oil and other business deals - the planned Hungarian purchase of Serbia's Nis oil refinery. The two nationalist leaders found much in common, in business and politics, not least their friendship with Vladimir Putin in Russia and Chinese President Xi Jinping, and their strong support for Milorad Dodik, the separatist leader of the Bosnian Serbs.
A high-speed railway between Belgrade and Budapest is being built with Chinese finance and know-how.
The parallels between the fall from power of the two men are extraordinary. Aleksandar VuÄiÄ admitted defeat at exactly 21:30 on Sunday evening, just as Viktor OrbÃ¡n did on 12 April. Few observers expected either leader to concede peacefully.
There has been speculation this week that VuÄiÄ spoke to OrbÃ¡n twice on Sunday night to ask his advice - once before he conceded, and again at 23:15. And that OrbÃ¡n convinced his Serbian ally not to use force.
VuÄiÄ denies that he spoke to OrbÃ¡n before he made his announcement, but acknowledges the later conversation. Viktor OrbÃ¡n, contacted by the BBC, declined to comment.
An hour before polls closed in Serbia, masked and hooded vigilantes took up position in central Belgrade. During voting, similar groups were photographed at many polling stations, and blocked by election monitors.
There is another strange numerical similarity. The Student List will have 140 seats in the 250-seat Serbian parliament, the same number PÃ©ter Magyar's Tisza party won in the 199-seat Hungarian parliament.
Magyar was the only European leader to ring the students directly to congratulate them that evening - and probably the only one who had their number.
"It is always good to hear that the story of Tisza could provide an inspiration for other nations," the Hungarian prime minister told the BBC.
"The result of the Hungarian election clearly showed us that what we are doing here is right," the head of the Student List, Ilija SrdanoviÄ, said on the eve of the vote.
SrdanoviÄ was one of those PÃ©ter Magyar spoke to that Sunday evening.
OrbÃ¡n, 63, and VuÄiÄ, 56, may now both face prosecution for corruption and abuse of power.
The judicial machinery in both countries is similar. Serbia's special prosecution service for organised crime, JTOK, and Hungary's brand new special prosecutors, known as NVVH, have similar powers. They could prove useful to each other.
Hungarian companies close to OrbÃ¡n were also involved in the Novi Sad railway station construction project. The collapse of the station's canopy on 1 November 2024 - blamed on corruption, as well as negligence - killed 16 people, and acted as the catalyst for the Serbian student movement.
"There was a perception in Europe that the longer the OrbÃ¡n and VuÄiÄ regimes stayed in office, the stronger they got," Ãron Timar, founder of the DE civic action group in Hungary told the BBC.
"In fact they got weaker. And once society found its voice and rose up, there was no way of stopping it."

Tens of thousands of people are expected to gather in the Indian capital, Delhi, for a mega opposition rally, seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner and electoral reforms.
The rally, called by the main opposition Congress party, will begin around noon at the famous Ramlila Maidan grounds, with leaders claiming a million people could attend.
Several top leaders of the Congress-led INDIA alliance have said they would attend and the influential Gen Z-led pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has also pledged support.
The rally comes amid growing criticism of a voter-list revision exercise that has removed 130 million names from the draft rolls across India.
The Election Commission of India (ECI) says the exercise is aimed at updating the voters' list by purging names of people who have died or moved away from their registered addresses.
But opposition parties allege that the exercise - known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) - could benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) by removing eligible voters from the rolls. They accuse the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the BJP of "vote chori (theft)". Both the BJP and the ECI have denied the allegations.
The controversy intensified in September when The Indian Express newspaper in its investigation, external reported that the CEC, Gyanesh Kumar, made key decisions related to the exercise without the agreement of the two other election commissioners, who had raised objections on more than a dozen occasions.
The Election Commission said differences of opinion were normal in any institution and did not affect its functioning.
But concerns over the revision process have continued, with the opposition parties, the CJP and student groups organising a number of protests in Delhi and other Indian cities.
Last month, Congress MP and leader of the opposition Rahul Gandhi led tens of thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place in central Delhi to the Supreme Court, seeking the CEC's resignation.
"The march was just the trailer," a party leader told the BBC, adding that "Sunday's rally will be several times bigger than that".
Ahead of the rally, Gandhi said their protest was against "the demolition of Indian democracy", adding that "all the opposition parties and everybody who wants to come, political or non-political, is welcome".
"There is huge anger, huge emotional pain because millions are being disenfranchised," he said.
"We are all standing together because we are defending the Constitution. We are defending the idea of India. We are defending the vote, which is the expression of all Indians."
Delhi police have given permission to hold Sunday's rally, but it comes with several conditions. Media reports say the rally must end by 5pm, CCTV cameras must be installed at the venue and no marches will be allowed outside the designated protest site.
The planned mega rally has also divided opinion among traders in Chandni Chowk, one of Delhi's oldest and busiest markets, located less than a kilometre from Ramlila Maidan.
Earlier this week, a group of traders said the protest could hurt business during the festive season, coming just a week before Diwali.
But a rival group of traders said they supported Gandhi's rally and criticised the BJP for taking out a march through the market on Thursday, saying that disrupted the festive season more.
Authorities have deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel across the city, including the roads leading up to Ramlila Grounds, Sunday's protest venue.
The opposition, which has been preparing for the rally for days now, has accused the government of trying to stop people from travelling to Delhi to take part in the protest.
Rahul Gandhi has appealed to people to turn up in large numbers. "Don't worry about the police, don't worry about lathis [batons] - the BJP will not have the guts to try any of their antics," he wrote on X.
His comments come amid growing concerns about the policing of recent protests in the capital.
On 10 October, thousands of security personnel were deployed and large parts of the city were shut down to thwart protests called by the CJP against CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
All of the top CJP leaders were detained and many demonstrators were beaten and dragged through the streets to break up their protests. BBC reporters covering demonstrations saw, external police dragging away protesters and using batons on some of them.
The CJP has publicly backed the INDIA bloc rally, but it is unclear whether its senior leaders will attend.

When Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific.
The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged".
Ranasingha had been hoping to settle in New Zealand.
After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa.
Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka.
Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed.
As a result, she has no feasible way of leaving.
"My son - my only child - is getting married in November and I really want to be there for his wedding. My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she says through tears.
"I will do anything they ask of me - I just want to go home."
Ranasingha left Sri Lanka in 2018 after being forced to close her small T-shirt factory due to a loss of business. Struggling to repay loans, she moved to Hong Kong to work as a domestic caregiver looking after elderly people and children.
Her brother tells BBC Sinhala she had come under immense financial pressure. Her husband was a drug addict who died about seven years ago, he adds.
In December 2022, Ranasingha headed to New Zealand, where she says she lived with a cousin on a two-month visit visa. As it came close to expiring, she says an immigration interpreter helped her apply for asylum on the grounds she was facing threats from lenders in Sri Lanka.
She was granted an asylum seeker "open work visa", enabling her to work for almost any employer for a year. She found a job at a restaurant, she says, which ultimately agreed to sponsor an employment visa, which she believed would give her longer-term stability.
But as asylum seekers generally cannot apply for other visas while their applications are processed in New Zealand, it was declined.
That's when she got in touch with Immigration & Secretarial Services, a firm she claims told her a fresh application for an employment visa could be made from overseas. Email correspondence the BBC has seen shows its manager, Sylviane Gallant, saying she would initiate the process as soon as Ranasingha had left the country.
So she booked a short stay in the Cook Islands while the application was made.
It turned out to be a disastrous decision.
She was again refused the employment visa. And by leaving New Zealand, she had violated the terms of her existing visa. New Zealand authorities made it clear they would not grant her any future visas.
Gallant claimed to make various interventions on her behalf, including writing to politicians including Chris Penk, New Zealand's then-immigration minister. But ultimately, Ranasingha says Gallant admitted the situation was her fault and told her "there was nothing more she could do".
"She told me I was better off going home. There was nothing holding me there so I agreed to go."
But when she turned up at the airport with an Air New Zealand ticket to Sri Lanka in hand, she was told she couldn't board the flight without a New Zealand transit visa.
Three applications for a New Zealand transit visa were rejected. Authorities said they weren't convinced she would leave New Zealand. Four applications for Australian transit visas were rejected too.
In one of its rejections, New Zealand suggested she explore other routes. But both the US state of Hawaii and the French Polynesian island of Tahiti told her she would need to provide biometric information before any visa could be processed - and that could only be done in person in New Zealand.
Her latest application to New Zealand, which included all the details of the alternative routes she'd been trying, as well as her son's upcoming wedding and mother's failing health, was also rejected.
"I have lost so much money on tickets. For almost four years I have been just applying for visa after visa with nothing working out," she says, breaking down.
On a collection of islands known for their sweeping sandy beaches and rugged volcanic peaks, just four hours from Auckland, Ranasingha has been an involuntary guest.
She's luckier than others in her position, she says, with her hotel letting her stay free of charge in its staff accommodation and friendly locals providing her with food and clothing.
One of the hotel directors even gave her a sewing machine, she says, enabling her to make a small income.
"My mother always tells me I must have done something good, for me to be in a place like this where people have been so kind to me," she tells the BBC.
But it does little to ease the sense of being trapped.
Ranasingha says the stress is impacting her health. "I am scared something is going to happen to me," she says.
"I don't know what her solution is, to be honest," says Auckland-based immigration law specialist Alastair McClymont.
She had received "terrible advice" which "certainly" could not have come from a genuine immigration lawyer, he says, pointing to an industry of "so-called immigration consultants" who charge people to lodge applications without fully understanding the risks involved. Ranasingha says she has parted with thousands of New Zealand dollars in fees to Immigration & Secretarial Services.
The BBC reached out to Gallant but did not receive a response.
McClymont suggests New Zealand authorities will not grant the transit visa because, as far as they are concerned, she has no intention of returning to Sri Lanka h

READ MORE: Justice Department seeks to isolate Alaska ballots as criminal probe underway over Senate candidate The scathing filing from the state's attorney general's office comes as U.S. District Court Judge Sharon L. Gleason set a deadline of Saturday for arguments over whether she should dismiss the lawsuit without even a hearing. The complaint from the U.S. Department of Justice has been roundly criticized by election law experts and demands that the judge halt certification of a possible win by Democrat Mary Peltola until it is determined whether voters were confused by the presence of a second candidate on the ballot with the same name as her main rival, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Department of Justice on Friday added a request that the judge separate all ballots showing votes for the second Dan Sullivan until it can be determined whether voters were fooled into wasting their votes for a spoiler candidate. In its Saturday filing, Alaska said this was "both disturbing and impossible." It added there would be no way to do that without violating voter privacy. Trump also demanded that Peltola be prosecuted after The New York Times this week reported that internal texts and posts appear to show the Democrats' campaign was involved in recruiting the second Sullivan, a retired school teacher in the remote fishing village of Petersburg, onto the ballot. But the state filing notes that the two Sullivans are distinguished from each other on the ballot — the senator is listed as a Republican and the incumbent, while the other simply as "Daniel J. Sullivan Jr." "State officials carefully designed the ballot to minimize voter confusion," Alaska officials wrote. "The Court should immediately dismiss this lawsuit with prejudice and allow state officials to conduct the general election — including ballot counting and certification — free from unwarranted federal interference." The Trump administration argued that a preamble to the 1990s law governing voter registration gave it the responsibility for ensuring states maintained the "integrity" of federal elections. The Department of Justice issued a wave of subpoenas and announced it was conducting a criminal investigation in the case as the administration has stepped up its use of its legal powers to support Trump's side in the midterm election. Peltola has denied involvement in the presence of the second Sullivan on the ballot. The Times report was based on interviews with her former campaign manager, texts and contributions from a political group backing Peltola to an out-of-state Democratic consultant who recruited the second Sullivan. The state government's filing on Saturday says that the new revelations about the possible role of Peltola's campaign don't change the fact that he's legally on the ballot. "Not every wrong can be righted in federal court," the state wrote. Peltola's campaign and voting rights groups also have urged Gleason to dismiss the case, putting them in unusual alignment with Alaska state officials. "Imagine if the federal executive could pluck a few words like 'election integrity' from some statutory preamble and, on that basis alone, bend the machinery of state elections to his will, preemptively blocking certification of a U.S. Senate election to protect his preferred candidate from defeat and then subjecting voters to a law-enforcement-led inquest about who they 'really' supported," the American Civil Liberties Union wrote in a filing urging the lawsuit's dismissal. A rare species of beetle has been found in Pembrokeshire after being missing from Wales for 60 years.
The Short-Necked Oil Beetle are dependent on solitary bees for its lifecycle and need a particular habitat to survive, with thick vegetation for shelter and dense flower coverage both essential.
They were not reported in the UK for almost 60 years after 1948 as habitat loss brought the species to the brink of extinction.
Anne Hobbs, from the Bumblebee Conservation Trust, said it was "very exciting" that the evidence suggested the species was breeding in Wales again.
Last year, the survey at Castlemartin found only dead adults of this particular beetle, raising concerns about the future of this species and its continued presence on the site.
But this year, after three years of searching, experts discovered larvae of the beetle on a small area of the site, suggesting that surveyors had managed to find some of the hatchlings from a larger batch of immature beetles.
The number and distribution of the beetle larvae seen also supported this, according to Natural Resources Wales (NRW).
The Short-Necked Oil Beetle is classed as nationally rare within Great Britain and listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, external.
They can typically be found from March to June in flower-rich coastal grassland and sand dune habitat, and are most active on warm, sunny days.
Adults can grow up toe 24mm (0.9in) in length and the life span of an adult is approximately one year.
NRW said these conditions mean there are only a handful of suitable sites in the UK.
They were rediscovered in Devon in 2006 and on the Isle of Coll, in Scotland, in 2009. Since then, populations have been found on Tiree, Islay, Barra and Uist.
Castlemartin Range, in Pembrokeshire, is currently the only place in Wales where the species can be found and it is being consistently surveyed by conservationists.
The project is part of Wales's "flagship species recovery programme", said NRW, which works to conserve the Short-Necked Oil Beetle Sand other species that share similar habitats.
Hobbs described the Short-Necked Oil Beetle as an "amazing creature" and said their work needed to consider the "needs of several species to be effective".
She thanked their partners and volunteers for their continued support, despite having two years without a larval sighting.
"We look forward to the continued management of the site so that this amazing species can survive now and into the future."

Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.
Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles.
Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.
The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.
As night fell, demonstrations turned violent.
A large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.
Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.
Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".
She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden."
On Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed. The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.
Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing trainers and other items, local media reported.
Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended.
Poseck said: "We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard."
Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.
Similar instances took place in other German cities, following earlier largely peaceful demonstrations.
In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.
Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was "sad and deeply saddening that young people who wanted to peacefully demonstrate for their future were infiltrated today by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind".
A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.
In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.
The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe.
In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.
Thousands of police officers were deployed across France to deal with the demonstrations, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 500 arrests after clashes in Toulouse, Lyon and Marseille.
French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail. Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.
Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.
In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.
Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.
While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.

Two rhino calves have celebrated their first birthday with cakes made of pellets, carrots and salad leaves.
Siblings Markus and Mo were born at Cotswold Wildlife Park, near Burford, last year.
The pair weighed about 70kg (11st) at birth, and now weigh about 500kg (78st) each. Their arrival took the number of rhinos at the park to nine, the most in its 56-year history.
White rhinos were close to extinction in the early 1900s, with fewer than 50 thought to remain in Africa. They are now the most numerous of the five rhino species, but the park says conservation remains vital.

A major recovery effort is continuing after an oil spill caused by the vandalism of a nearby home heating oil tank resulted in the death of 13 birds from Broughshane Waterfowl Park.
More than 20 birds were transported to the USPCA's headquarters last week for urgent specialist care, but the death toll has continued to rise.
The popular attraction in County Antrim has been forced to close while efforts continue to remove oil from the pond.
Police have appealed for anyone with information to come forward.
Broughshane Environment Wildfowl and Wildlife Trust's chairman, Gary Hayward, said they incident had been a "nightmare".
"We are devastated," he told BBC News NI.
"One of our volunteers appeared on the Thursday morning to feed [the birds], and walked down through the park and smelt this kerosene smell and saw the black swans completely oiled."
The park is home to 120 "collection birds", as well as wild birds, he explained.
"So far we have lost 13 birds, some of which are really close to us."
Hayward praised the efforts of the USPCA and Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA), who have been instrumental in treating the sick birds and clearing up the spillage.
The Northern Ireland Environment Agency (NIEA) was first alerted to the incident on Thursday 22 October and have been involved in trying to remove the oil waste.
"The incident was quickly confirmed as having had a significant impact on the ponds and NIEA inspectors deployed oil absorbent booms and other countermeasures as mitigation," a spokesperson said.
The agency said the substance involved had been identified as home heating oil, or kerosene, and that the source had been traced to a nearby tank.
The waterway is noted to be much improved but further works will be carried out as long as is deemed necessary.
Hayward hopes that the incident will be an deterrent to those engaged in vandalism.
"People need to be fully aware of what impact it can have if somebody vandalises a heating containers and tanks."
Siobhan Hawthorn, wildlife supervisor at the USPCA, has been a key part of the rescue operation.
"It's massively frustrating when these kind of incidents occur, especially when it's caused by carelessness and us humans and these poor birds have suffered because of it," she said.
"There's no reason for them to have died needlessly for that reason."
Siobhan and the team have been working tirelessly to help revive the birds which include geese, ducks and swans.
"It's been a case of getting them all bathed and treated as soon as we could because of the level of contamination they suffered," she said.
"We've given them all doses of charcoal to help combat some of the toxins that they would have ingested.
"Unfortunately not all of them got to us as quickly as we would have liked and they have ingested too much," she added.
Siobhan and the team said the incident has also placed their staff under considerable pressure "emotionally and mentally".
The centre is unsure just how long they will have to care for the remaining birds.
"We would like to think that they're over the worst of it, but you just don't know exactly how much they have potentially ingested," she explained.
"Birds are extremely good at hiding illnesses and ailments, so sometimes you don't see the symptoms until it's a little bit too late because they're just so good at hiding it.
"The majority of these birds that have come into us are actually not native species so they can't be returned until the pond is 100% fully cleaned and cleared."

As a child growing up in Slovenia in 1999, Dr Rok NeÅ¾iÄ couldn't have known that an asteroid that was discovered in New Mexico that year would be named after him almost three decades later.
The Orchard County may be best known for its apples, but for NeÅ¾iÄ the real attraction was astronomy.
He first arrived to Armagh Observatory and Planetarium (AOP) in 2015 to complete his doctorate in space and climate physics, and has remained there ever since.
More than a decade on, he is one of two AOP employees to have recently been chosen to have a celestial body named after them.
NeÅ¾iÄ, who works at the planetarium as a tours and outreach officer, said he thought it was "so cool" when he learned that asteroids can be named after people.
Speaking to BBC News NI, NeÅ¾iÄ said he wished he "could get there some day" and, now that he has, he described it as "a dream come true".
"I'm not sure how to believe it myself,â he admitted.
He explains that an asteroid is "a smallish rock in space" compared to planets, and that his one is named (20560) NeÅ¾iÄ., external
"That's its official name, so the number there tells you basically the order of discovery."
It is currently "sitting safely out in the asteroid belt and just going around the Sun, just like we are", he explained.
The naming process for small bodies in the solar system is governed by the International Astronomical Union, external. Asteroids can be named by their discoverers once their orbits are sufficiently known.
NeÅ¾iÄ's asteroid is 10.9km across, while that belonging to his colleague Shane Kelly is 15.6km.
"They're both actually quite large as far as these asteroids that are named after people tend to be, because most of the really large ones were discovered first," NeÅ¾iÄ said.
"So they were named a long time ago, and now we're finding smaller and smaller ones."
NeÅ¾iÄ's asteroid was discovered by "one of the big missions", he said.
"This is an Earth-based mission in this case, which is looking for lots of asteroids, essentially, because the more we know about them, the more we know where they're going, the more we know which ones are not hitting us, including mine and Shane's."
To be considered for an asteroid namesake, someone must nominate you, and in NeÅ¾iÄ's case, two people put his name forward.
He doesn't know who chose him for the honour - but his PhD supervisor, and a former astronomer from the observatory nominated him.
NeÅ¾iÄ focused on comets with polarised light for his studies and years later is "still" talking about space.
The planetarium and observatory is "punching well above our weight", he said.
"Even though we're a small institution, people who work here can just focus on the research so much that we have really top researchers in the field."
The planetarium's neighbouring observatory has monitored the weather for more than than 230 years.
Shane Kelly, who is the principal meteorological observer at Armagh Observatory, was nominated by the emeritus director.
Since 1999, his role involves opening what is known as the Stevenson screen which holds sensitive thermometers, before noting down his readings for the day into the handwritten ledger.
His hand has entered far more lines of data than any of his 17 predecessors and his asteroid is called (7050) Shanekelly.
Kelly has been "doing this for 27 years", the institute's director said.
"He's probably observed the weather more than anyone else in the world, I suspect," Prof Michael Burton said.
"So this is in recognition of Shane's contribution to the observatory and to the measuring of the weather."
Kelly's asteroid was discovered in Chile, external in 1982.
Burton said it's "fantastic" that the two members of the team have been awarded in this way.
"There are now 29 asteroids which have some connection with the observatory and planetarium here in Armagh."
The AOP now plans on recognising their achievements with a new LED dome, which will show the asteroids and their orbits.

An endangered damselfly has been spotted in wetlands created by an "ambitious" project that restored a stretch of a rare chalk river.
The scare blue-tailed damselfly, one of the world's earliest flying insect species, was recorded alongside the River Ash near Hertford.
The 4.3-mile (7km) stretch at the Easneye Estate was restored to its original course last year.
The Herts and Middlesex Wildlife Trust said that for species facing increasing pressure, creating and restoring suitable habitats was "vital to reversing declines".
The scarce blue-tailed damselfly was recorded at two monitoring sites located close together in late summer.
A new assessment of Britain's dragonflies and damselflies highlighted growing concerns about the future of some species.
The British Dragonfly Society's Red List, external review reclassified the scarce blue-tailed damselfly from Near Threatened to Endangered.
It found that eight species were now classed as endangered, twice the number identified in the previous assessment in 2008.
The River Ash is one of about 260 chalk rivers in the world, and the restoration project has included the creation of new gravel beds.
The trust said brown trout were already spawning on them.
In addition, monitoring carried out before and after the restoration found an increase in river invertebrates, including mayflies and stoneflies.
Sarah Perry, rivers recovery manager at the trust said: "Natural rivers, connected floodplains and healthy wetlands support biodiversity by providing places for wildlife to feed and breed.
"They also help water move through the landscape and can contribute to resilience against both flooding and drought.
"The scarce blue-tailed damselfly sightings along the River Ash offer a hopeful example of what these efforts can achieve."

The race for a US Senate seat in Texas may prove crucial in determining which party controls Congress next year â a significant prize in its own right - but for both parties it represents so much more than that.
For the Democrats, their losing streak in statewide elections now stretches back more than three decades. In the second most populous state in America, liberals have been in the wilderness for a generation.
But polls suggest their candidate, 37-year-old James Talarico, may be on the verge of breaking through and turning a Texas Senate seat blue for the first time since 1988.
That would be a dream scenario for Democrats - and a potential nightmare for Republicans.
"If the Democrats do pull it off, I think it's going to cause a lot of soul searching and a lot of psychological damage to the Republican Party in Texas and nationwide," said Brendan Steinhauser, a Texas-based Republican campaign strategist.
These dramatic stakes help explain how this Senate race has rocketed to become the most expensive in US history, with total spending reaching more than half a billion dollars.
For Talarico, it has been a remarkable rise for a candidate who in 2025 was a relatively unknown state-level Democrat.
At the Fiesta Center in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday night, the line to see the softly spoken former teacher, who studied to be a Christian minister, stretched around the building and down the wide parking lot to a busy road.
In this dusty western plains town of about 250,000, which voted overwhelmingly for President Donald Trump two years ago, a visit from a major Democratic candidate on the eve of an election was unusual.
"It's just so amazing to watch," said Aaron Gonzalez, the Democratic Party chair for Hockley County, which borders Lubbock. "This time is different."
When Talarico took the stage before an estimated 3,000 supporters â with another thousand listening on speakers outside - his pitch was a familiar one for many national Democrats this year, albeit with a Texas twist.
He railed against a conservative political establishment that he said is insensitive to the economic hardship of average Americans. He condemned the corrosive influence of big money in politics. And he promised to advance a "comprehensive anti-corruption agenda" in the Senate.
"Texans are ready for change," he said. "We are done with the extremism and the corruption. We're done with the politics of division, and we are ready for something new."
The slogan for his final two weeks of campaigning â "clear eyes, full hearts, can't lose" â is taken from Friday Night Lights, a popular early 2000s TV show about a plucky small-town Texas high school football team.
His music playlist leans heavily on twangy Texas country music. He celebrates Texas breakfast tacos, quotes legendary Texas singer-songwriter Lyle Lovett and frequently mentions that his ties to the state go back eight generations.
In the Lubbock audience, Andrew Robinson, a student from nearby Texas Tech University, liked what he heard. But the 26-year-old's optimism was tempered by an entire lifetime spent watching Democrats try, and fail, to get a toehold in the state.
"A Talarico win would mean so much," he said. "I haven't been keen on wanting to stay in Texas. And if the government were to change, it could give me a reason."
For Republicans, a Democratic win in Texas would have a very different meaning.
At roughly the same time Talarico was addressing his supporters in the Fiesta Center, Trump â alongside the Republican Party's Senate candidate Ken Paxton â was just a few miles away, in a venue twice the size.
"If you go out and vote, we're going to have a tremendous win in Texas," the president told the crowd.
Trump's visit to reliably-Republican Lubbock suggests the party is concerned about turnout even in the most conservative portions of the state. It is a worry that has been echoed by other Texas Republicans.
"Understand, we could lose Texas," Texas Senator Ted Cruz said in his podcast on Friday. "The Democrats are massively out-turning-out the Republicans."
Don Huffines, who is running for election as the state's chief financial officer, issued an even more dire warning. "Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America," he posted on X.
"When the foundation breaks, it all falls apart. When we lose Texas, we lose the USA."
For weeks now, party leaders have been warning that a liberal breakthrough in the Lone Star State could have dire consequences.
They fear a Talarico win would motivate more local Democrats to run for statewide and federal offices. Better quality candidates with more funding could lead to a snowball effect similar to the Democratic inroads seen in other southern states, such as Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia.
"I think that it's pretty clear that Republicans, especially candidates, consultants, operatives, and others who are active in the party, see that this is a real threat," said Steinhauser.
"The days of waving this off and saying that Texas would never turn blue are over."
For the Texas Senate race to come to the point where recent polls suggest Talarico has a slim but stable lead has required a unique confluence of events and political dynamics â a "perfect storm", in the words of Steinhauser.
"Everything that could go well for the Democrats is going well," he said, "and everything that could go badly for the Republicans is going badly."
But it is also a whirlwind that, in a significant part, has been sown over the past year by Trump himself.
The national environment for Republicans is a harsh one.
Voters are frustrated with high consumer costs, including the price of petrol, and largely blame Trump's tariff policies and the Iran war.
Political corruption has become an issue of growing concern. Democrats, independents and many Republicans in a recent Cook political report poll identified "greedy billionaires and corporations" and politicians seeking "personal gain" as the ones to blame.

Watch: Heidi Klum as giant severed hand for Halloween bash
The supermodel and TV host Heidi Klum continued her pose as the queen of Halloween by transforming into a giant, bloodied and severed hand for her annual costume party on 31 October.
Klum, 53, was completely unrecognisable arriving at her event in what she described as her own chopped-off "left hand".
